entries.meaning: Names an indefinite small count of two or three, in Upper Midwestern and casual American speech.
examples: Give me a couple three days and I'll have the estimate.
"There was a couple three guys out front waiting on you."
We're two-three weeks out from opening, tops.
He pulled a couple two three beers out of the cooler and sat down.
It's a couple three miles up the county road, past the silo.
In writing, make it two or three: ✗ a couple three days → ✓ two or three days.
entries.pronunciation note: a is weak, /ə/, and in running speech couple loses its /l/ into the number — a couple three days is usually /ə ˈkʌpə ˈθri ˈdeɪz/; the fuller a couple two three /ə ˈkʌpəl tu ˈθri/ runs all three numbers together with no pause
entries.русский: пара-тройка — разг., регионализм Среднего Запада: два-три
entries.position: a quantity phrase filling the determiner slot of a bare plural noun; nothing central may join it
entries.register: regional and colloquial — Upper Midwestern and Great Lakes speech above all (Wisconsin, Minnesota, Michigan, Chicago), where it passes unnoticed in conversation, and casual speech more widely. It is not standard written English and appears in print only in dialogue.
entries.type: cardinal numeral (indefinite small count, = two or three)
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — a couple three days, a couple three guys. Never a singular countable noun (✗ a couple three day) and never an uncountable noun (✗ a couple three water → a couple three glasses of water).
entries.with of: No of before a bare plural noun — a couple three beers — and speakers who use this construction drop of from plain a couple too (a couple beers). Of returns before a determiner or a pronoun: a couple three of the guys, a couple three of them.
entries.pattern: a couple three [plural noun] · a couple two three [plural noun] · two-three [plural noun] · a couple three of [the/my + plural noun] · a couple three (standing alone)
entries.contrast: This is two or three with the or worn away, and the stacked a couple two three is one of the clearest markers of Upper Midwestern speech. The count is genuinely approximate — nobody saying it is promising three. In writing, use two or three, or a couple of, which is the neutral form of the same idea. Against a few: a few is vaguer and can run to five or six, while a couple three stays pinned at two or three. Agreement is plain plural: A couple three guys were waiting.
entries.variants: a couple two three, two-three, two or three, a couple of, a few
entries.see also: a couple of, a few, one or two, two, three, four, one or more

entries.meaning: A hundred and forty-four of something, counted as one wholesale unit.
examples: The order sheet says a gross of number-two pencils.
They shipped two gross of machine screws in the wrong size.
We go through a gross of zip ties a month at the shop.
Half a gross of envelopes will cover the whole mailing.
The invoice reads 3 gross, which is four hundred thirty-two units.
Outside a stockroom nobody says a gross of anything — they say 144.
entries.pronunciation note: a /ə/ and of /əv/ are weak; the vowel is the /oʊ/ of grow, and the s is voiceless — /ɡroʊs/, never ✗ /ɡroʊz/
entries.русский: гросс — 144 штуки, дюжина дюжин (торг., в накладных и каталогах)
entries.position: a is the central determiner of gross; the whole phrase heads a partitive
entries.register: trade and wholesale — purchase orders, invoices, and stationery and hardware catalogs. An American who has never worked a stockroom may never meet it, and in ordinary prose 144 is clearer.
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns, and only the small manufactured things that are actually sold by the gross — a gross of pencils, two gross of screws, a gross of buttons. Never an uncountable noun (✗ a gross of water) and never a singular countable noun (✗ a gross of pencil).
entries.with of: Required in the ordinary a gross of pencils — ✗ a gross pencils. As with dozen, the order desk drops it when a number governs a bare plural (ten gross envelopes), but ten gross of envelopes is the safer written form. Of is required before a determiner or a pronoun: a gross of the small ones, a gross of them.
entries.pattern: a gross of [plural noun] · [cardinal] gross of [plural noun] · half a gross of [plural noun] · a great gross of [plural noun] (= 1,728, effectively dead) · by the gross
entries.contrast: The count word stays singular under a number, exactly like dozen and hundred: two gross of screws, never ✗ two grosses of screws. Unlike dozen, though, gross has no everyday life left outside the supply room, so write 144 unless you are quoting an invoice. Do not confuse the numeral with the far commoner adjective gross meaning "before deductions" (gross income, gross weight) or the slang gross meaning disgusting — same spelling, unrelated words. Agreement follows the plural noun: A gross of pencils were delivered.
entries.variants: two gross, half a gross, a great gross (= 1,728), a dozen dozen, by the gross, 144
entries.see also: dozen, a pair of, score, hundred, thousand, million, billion

entries.meaning: Names a comically large, uncounted number — hyperbole rather than arithmetic.
examples: There are a jillion reasons not to refinance right now.
I've got a zillion emails and not one that needs answering.
Mama's told you forty-eleven times to stay off that porch rail.
Jillions of mosquitoes came off the river after the rain.
He's got forty-eleven cousins scattered between here and Knoxville.
That's a bazillion dollars in equipment sitting in an unlocked shed.
entries.pronunciation note: a is weak, /ə/, exactly as in a million; the variant forty-eleven is /ˌfɔrti ɪˈlɛvən/, FOR-tee-ih-LEV-uhn, with the main beat on -lev-
entries.русский: тьма, вагон, мильон — сленг, гипербола: несметное количество, никогда буквально
entries.position: postdeterminer, in the same slot as million, after a
entries.register: slang and hyperbolic, never literal. A jillion, a zillion, and a bazillion are ordinary American informal speech and writing — texts, complaints, sports talk. Forty-eleven is narrower: Southern and Appalachian folk speech, often addressed to a child, and it sounds regional to everyone else. None of them belongs anywhere a real number is being reported.
entries.type: cardinal numeral (hyperbolic indefinite — an uncountably large number)
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns — a jillion reasons, forty-eleven forms. Never a singular countable noun (✗ a jillion reason) and never an uncountable noun (✗ a jillion homework → a jillion assignments).
entries.with of: No of before a bare plural noun: a jillion reasons. Of is required before a determiner or a pronoun (a jillion of those forms, a jillion of them), and the plural jillions of always takes it, exactly like millions of.
entries.pattern: a jillion [plural noun] · jillions of [plural noun] · forty-eleven [plural noun] · a jillion times · a zillion / bazillion / gazillion [plural noun]
entries.contrast: These are not numbers; they are complaints and boasts wearing a number's clothes, which is why nothing that measures can sit beside them: ✗ about a jillion, ✗ a jillion and six, ✗ at least a jillion. umpteen is the same idea one register up, and the matching ordinals live at nth, umpteenth. Forty-eleven is built the way a child builds a big number — a real ten stacked on a real teen — and that is its flavor in Southern speech: I've told you forty-eleven times. Agreement is plain plural: A jillion things are wrong with it.
entries.variants: a zillion, a bazillion, a gazillion, a kajillion, jillions of, forty-eleven (Southern and Appalachian), umpteen, a hundred and one
entries.see also: hundred, thousand, million, billion, nth, umpteenth, umpteen, countless, dozens of

entries.meaning: Counts a noun that has no singular of its own, or one that comes in twos, by counting the units instead.
examples: I need a pair of scissors that actually cuts.
She bought two pairs of jeans and returned both.
Do you have a pair of pliers in the truck?
A pair of glasses was sitting on the dashboard.
There isn't a pair of clean socks left in the house.
He owns exactly one pair of dress shoes.
A pair of twins joined the class in October.
entries.pronunciation note: both a /ə/ and of /əv/ are weak and unstressed; only pair carries a beat
entries.русский: пара — два предмета; счётное слово для парных существительных: брюки, ножницы
entries.position: a is the central determiner of pair; the whole phrase heads a partitive
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: cardinal numeral (unit counter, = two, and the counter for plural-only nouns)
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — either a plural-only noun that has no singular at all (a pair of scissors, a pair of pants, a pair of glasses, a pair of tweezers) or an ordinary noun naming things that come in twos (a pair of shoes, a pair of gloves, a pair of twins). Never a singular countable noun (✗ a pair of shoe) and never an uncountable noun (✗ a pair of water, ✗ a pair of advice).
entries.with of: Required and fixed — ✗ a pair scissors. A second of builds a partitive on top: a pair of the good scissors, two of the pairs I bought.
entries.pattern: a pair of [plural noun] · [cardinal] pairs of [plural noun] · this/that pair of [plural noun] · another pair of [plural noun] · a pair of [pronoun] (rare)
entries.contrast: This is the only way to count a plural-only noun. Scissors, pants, jeans, shorts, glasses, pliers, tweezers, and binoculars have no singular form, so a cardinal cannot touch them directly: two scissors, ✗ one pant, ✗ three jeans. The number counts the pairs instead — two pairs of scissors, one pair of pants. ✗ Agreement follows pair, not the noun after of: One pair of scissors is missing, Two pairs of scissors are missing — but the bare noun by itself stays plural, The scissors are missing, never ✗ The scissors is missing. With ordinary countables, a pair of means exactly two where a couple of means roughly two.
entries.variants: pairs of, a set of, a couple of (approximate two), a brace of (game birds, archaic), pant / scissor (attributive singulars only: a pant leg, a scissor kick)
entries.see also: two, three, four, dozen, a couple of, several, both

entries.meaning: Twelve of something, counted as a unit.
examples: Pick up a dozen eggs on your way home.
They ordered three dozen chairs for the reception.
Half a dozen people had already complained.
Dozens of flights were canceled before noon.
I've read a dozen of these reports and they all say the same thing.
She sent two dozen roses and no note.
We don't have a dozen chairs, let alone three dozen.
entries.pronunciation note: the article in front is weak: a dozen /ə ˈdʌzən/, never ✗ /eɪ ˈdʌzən/
entries.русский: дюжина — двенадцать; после числа без -s: two dozen eggs
entries.position: postdeterminer, after a, the, a possessive, or another cardinal
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns — a dozen eggs, two dozen roses. Not uncountable nouns (✗ a dozen water → a dozen bottles of water) and not singular countable nouns (✗ a dozen egg).
entries.with of: No of before a bare plural noun: a dozen eggs, ✗ a dozen of eggs. Of is required before a determiner or a pronoun: a dozen of the eggs, a dozen of them. The plural dozens always takes of: dozens of complaints.
entries.pattern: a/one dozen [plural noun] · [cardinal] dozen [plural noun] · a dozen of [the/my/these + plural noun] · dozens of [plural noun] · half a dozen [plural noun]
entries.contrast: Like hundred and thousand, dozen stays singular when a number counts it — two dozen eggs, never ✗ two dozens eggs. It goes plural only when the count is vague and of follows: dozens of eggs. The same rule governs score (twenty), which survives mainly in four score and seven. Agreement follows the plural noun: A dozen eggs were on the counter. And dozen doubles as a pronoun — as a determiner it precedes a noun (a dozen eggs), as a pronoun it stands alone (I'll take a dozen, he sent two dozen).
entries.variants: half a dozen, a baker's dozen (thirteen), dozens of, score (= twenty, archaic)
entries.see also: a pair of, hundred, thousand, million, billion, a couple of, two, three, four

entries.meaning: A round large number used to count a plural noun. Note on and. The standard American reading of 253 is two hundred fifty-three; two hundred and fifty-three is standard British and perfectly acceptable in the United States. Keep and for the decimal point in dictation (two hundred and five tenths) and out of whole numbers in American technical writing.
examples: The city issued two hundred fifty permits last month.
A thousand things could go wrong between now and Friday.
Hundreds of commuters were stranded at the station.
The settlement came to four million dollars.
Only three hundred of the tickets were ever sold.
She has a hundred and one reasons not to go.
entries.pronunciation note: the article in front is weak — a hundred /ə ˈhʌndrəd/, a million /ə ˈmɪljən/; the full one hundred /ˈwʌn ˈhʌndrəd/ is the stressed, precise alternative
entries.русский: сто, тысяча, миллион, миллиард — после числительного без -s: three hundred
entries.position: postdeterminer
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns — a hundred reasons, two million dollars. Never an uncountable noun directly (✗ a thousand water → a thousand gallons of water) and never a singular countable noun (✗ a hundred reason).
entries.with of: No of before a bare plural noun: three hundred people, ✗ three hundred of people. Of is required before a determiner or a pronoun (three hundred of the applicants, a million of them) and after the plural forms (hundreds of people, thousands of dollars).
entries.pattern: a/one hundred [plural noun] · [cardinal] hundred [plural noun] · [cardinal] hundred [cardinal] [plural noun] · hundreds of [plural noun] · [cardinal] hundred of [the/my + plural noun]
entries.contrast: The singular rule is the whole entry. When a number governs them they never take -s: three hundred people, five thousand miles, two million dollars — ✗ three hundreds people. The -s form exists only for an indefinite, uncounted quantity, and it always requires of: hundreds of people, millions of dollars. Compare dozen, which behaves identically. Agreement splits the same way it does for the small cardinals: a plural count takes a plural verb (Two hundred permits were issued), but a sum of money, a distance, or a stretch of time treated as one amount takes a singular (Two million dollars is a lot to write off, Five thousand miles is a long way to drive).
entries.variants: one hundred (precise, formal), a hundred (ordinary), hundreds of, a hundred and one (idiomatic "very many"), trillion, zillion (informal)
entries.see also: dozen, two, three, four, percent, a couple of

entries.meaning: Counts exactly one of something, as opposed to any other number.
examples: The number. Exactly one, in contrast to any other number.
The emphatic singular. The one + noun singles out a unique member: the one thing I asked for.
"A certain." Formal, slightly legal or literary: One Robert Hayes has filed a claim.
One witness changed her story twice.
I'll be there in one hour, two at the most.
One of the elevators has been out since March.
That's the one mistake we can't afford to make.
Give me one good reason to stay.
One Mr. Delgado called while you were out.
entries.pronunciation note: it has no weak form. One keeps its full stressed vowel every time, which is exactly what separates it from the article: an hour /ən ˈaʊɚ/ against one hour /ˈwʌn ˈaʊɚ/. If the syllable reduces to /ə/ or /ən/, the word was a/an, not one.
entries.русский: один — числительное; после the значит «единственный»: the one exception
entries.position: postdeterminer as a numeral (the one exception); functions alone as the determiner of a bare noun phrase (one reason)
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns only — one reason, one child. Never a plural countable noun (✗ one reasons) and never an uncountable noun (✗ one information → one piece of information).
entries.with of: Required before a determiner or a pronoun, and the following noun is plural while the verb stays singular: one of the students was late, one of them. Never ✗ one of student.
entries.pattern: one [singular noun] · the/my/this one [singular noun] · one of [the/my/these + plural noun] · one of [pronoun] · one [singular noun] or another
entries.contrast: One against a/an is the core contrast. Both precede a singular countable noun, but one counts and a merely introduces: I waited an hour reports duration, I waited one hour insists it was exactly one and not two. Use a unless the number is the point. Note also that one is a pronoun (I'll take the red one, One never knows) — as a determiner it precedes a noun, as a pronoun it stands alone.
entries.variants: one and only, one or two, one another, the one (emphatic), a one (informal: that's a one)
entries.see also: a, two, three, four, first, another, once

entries.meaning: Sets a floor of one with no ceiling above it: at least one, possibly many.
examples: The form must be signed by one or more witnesses.
Coverage lapses if one or more of the conditions are not met.
Each account may be linked to one or more devices.
The statute applies wherever one or more parties reside in the state.
Check one or more of the boxes below.
One or more of the sensors were reporting bad data all week.
entries.pronunciation note: or is weak here, /ɚ/, and never carries a beat; one and more both keep their full vowels — the phrase is two stresses with a schwa between them
entries.русский: один или более — юр./тех. формула со значением «не менее одного»
entries.position: fills the determiner slot of a bare plural noun; it admits no central determiner in front of it (✗ the one or more copies)
entries.register: formal, legal, and technical — statutes, standards, specifications, and software documentation, where it is the standard way to write "at least one." It is stiff in conversation, which prefers one or two or some.
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns — one or more witnesses, one or more of the following conditions. Never a singular countable noun (✗ one or more witness) and never an uncountable noun (✗ one or more evidence → one or more pieces of evidence).
entries.with of: Required before a determiner or a pronoun, and the noun after of stays plural: one or more of the conditions, one or more of them, one or more of the following.
entries.pattern: one or more [plural noun] · one or more of [the/these + plural noun] · one or more of the following · of one or more [plural noun] · one or more (standing alone)
entries.contrast: The verb goes plural, which surprises everyone who sees one first: One or more of the panels are loose, If one or more conditions are met…. That is the reverse of one of, where the verb is singular (one of the panels is loose) — coordinating with more is what pluralizes it. Against at least one, which means the same thing in plainer words but takes a singular noun (at least one witness): drafters who want the plural noun reach for one or more. Against one or two, a casual estimate with a ceiling on it, this one has no ceiling at all. In plain-language editing, one or more of the following is usually just any of the following.
entries.variants: at least one, one or two, any of, one or more of the following, ≥ 1 (technical)
entries.see also: one, at least, at most, one or two, any, two, three, four

entries.meaning: Twenty of something counted as a unit — an archaic collective numeral surviving in scripture, oratory, and quotation.
examples: Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent a new nation.
The days of our years are threescore years and ten. (Psalm 90, King James Version)
He had been dead a score of years before anyone opened the trunk.
Fourscore militiamen answered the muster that morning.
Scores of protesters gathered outside the statehouse — the only form still in ordinary use.
Write twenty, not a score of, unless you are quoting somebody.
entries.pronunciation note: the article in front is weak: a score of years /ə ˈskɔr əv ˈjɪrz/; in the compounds the stress stays on the first element, threescore /ˈθriskɔr/, fourscore /ˈfɔrskɔr/
entries.русский: двадцать — устар., книжн.: four score and seven — восемьдесят семь
entries.position: postdeterminer, after a, the, or another cardinal
entries.register: archaic and literary. An American meets it in three places and almost nowhere else: the King James Bible (threescore and ten), the Gettysburg Address (Four score and seven years ago), and the living journalistic plural scores of, which no longer means twenty at all. Using it for a real count of twenty is a period costume.
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns — fourscore years, a score of witnesses. Never an uncountable noun (✗ a score of water) and never a singular countable noun (✗ a score of year).
entries.none in the old bare use: fourscore years, threescore and ten. Of is normal once the indefinite article appears — a score of years, a score of witnesses — and it is obligatory with the modern vague plural, scores of complaints.
entries.pattern: [cardinal] score [plural noun] · a score of [plural noun] · threescore and ten · fourscore and seven · scores of [plural noun] (modern)
entries.contrast: It stays singular under a number, like dozen and hundred: four score years, ✗ four scores years. The -s belongs only to the vague modern plural, which always takes of. Threescore (60) and fourscore (80) are single words frozen inside their famous phrases — threescore and ten is the biblical span of a life, seventy years, and fourscore and seven is eighty-seven. Note that score keeps a whole separate life as an ordinary noun — a tally, a grudge, a piece of written music — and none of that is a determiner.
entries.variants: threescore (= 60), fourscore (= 80), a score of, scores of (modern, vague), twoscore, three score and ten
entries.see also: dozen, a gross of, scores of, hundred, thousand, million, billion, twain

entries.meaning: The archaic form of two, surviving only after its noun, in fixed phrases, and in quotation.
examples: …and they twain shall be one flesh. (Matthew 19:5, King James Version)
Oh, East is East, and West is West, and never the twain shall meet.
The veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom.
He took his soundings and called "mark twain" — two fathoms, safe water.
In older verse the number follows the noun: days twain for two days.
Nothing in modern American English lets it stand in front of a noun: ✗ twain days → ✓ two days.
entries.pronunciation note: one syllable, rhyming with rain; there is no weak form — twain is always fully stressed, which is part of why it survives only inside set phrases
entries.русский: два, двое — устар., поэт.; стоит после существительного: in twain — надвое
entries.position: postpositive or fused-head — it follows its noun (days twain) or stands alone after a determiner (the twain, in twain). It does not sit in front of a noun in any living construction.
entries.register: archaic and literary. An American meets it in the King James Bible (they twain shall be one flesh), in Kipling (never the twain shall meet), in the frozen cut in twain, and in Mark Twain's pen name, taken from the leadsman's river cry mark twain — two fathoms. Nowhere else.
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns, and only in the archaic postpositive frame — brethren twain, days twain. It cannot precede a noun: ✗ twain days, ✗ twain reasons. As a fused head it takes the or they and stands alone: the twain, they twain.
entries.with of: Does not take of. The surviving phrases carry prepositions instead: in twain, between the twain.
entries.pattern: [plural noun] twain (archaic postpositive) · the twain (fused head) · in twain (= into two pieces) · they twain (biblical) · mark twain (river sounding)
entries.contrast: This is two in the shape two used to have. English once had more than one form of the numeral, and twain is the survivor of the one used when the number stood after its noun or alone — which is exactly why it never occupies a determiner slot the way two, three, four does. Days twain is a poetic inversion of two days, not a different determiner, and never the twain shall meet is a fused-head pronoun meaning "the two of them." Do not treat it as a fancy synonym you can drop into ordinary prose: outside quotation and deliberate pastiche it reads as costume.
entries.variants: two (the living form), in twain, the twain, they twain, mark twain (two fathoms), both
entries.see also: two, three, four, both, score, a pair of, one

entries.meaning: Any exact number above one, counting a plural noun.
examples: Three witnesses gave two conflicting accounts.
The first two chapters are free; after that you pay.
She ran twenty-six miles in four hours.
Two of the panelists never showed up.
We're taking a three-day weekend at the end of the month.
Five years is a long time to hold a grudge.
entries.pronunciation note: the numbers are always stressed, but the function words around them are not: three of the witnesses is /ˈθri əv ðə ˈwɪtnəsəz/, with of /əv/ and the /ðə/ both reduced
entries.русский: два, три, четыре — количественные числительные; идут после артикля и после порядкового
entries.position: postdeterminer — it follows any central determiner and follows an ordinal
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — two witnesses, three days. Never a singular countable noun (✗ two witness) and never an uncountable noun (✗ three information, ✗ four advice → three pieces of information, four pieces of advice). The one systematic exception is the hyphenated premodifier, where the noun goes singular: a three-day weekend, a two-mile run, a six-foot fence.
entries.with of: No of before a bare plural noun: three witnesses. Of is required before a determiner or a pronoun: three of the witnesses, two of them, four of my clients.
entries.pattern: [cardinal] [plural noun] · the/my/these [cardinal] [plural noun] · the [ordinal] [cardinal] [plural noun] · [cardinal] of [the/my/these + plural noun] · a [cardinal]-[singular measure noun] [noun]
entries.nonstandard: them two, them three (them two guys never showed) replaces the demonstrative those with object-form them; it is widespread in casual and regional American speech and is not standard written English — see them.
entries.contrast: Ordinal before cardinal, always: the first two questions, ✗ the two first questions; her last three albums, ✗ her three last albums. And note the agreement split: a plural count takes a plural verb (Three years have passed since then), but a measured quantity treated as one unit takes a singular (Three years is a long time to wait, Twenty miles is too far to walk). Nouns that are permanently plural — scissors, pants, glasses, tweezers — cannot be counted directly at all (✗ two scissors); they take a pair of, and the number counts the pairs: two pairs of scissors.
entries.variants: twenty-one through ninety-nine (hyphenated), two-and-a-half, a pair of (with permanently plural nouns), nought/naught (rare), them two (nonstandard)
entries.see also: one, a pair of, hundred, thousand, million, billion, first, third, fourth, fifth, many

entries.meaning: Names an absence of quantity as a counted amount rather than as a plain denial.
examples: The district has a zero tolerance policy for weapons.
This brand advertises zero calories and zero sugar.
She had zero interest in relitigating the argument.
The forecast calls for zero chance of rain through Sunday.
Two of the sensors reported zero degrees overnight.
There were zero injuries, which the chief called a miracle.
entries.русский: ноль, нулевой — нулевое количество; в отличие от прочих чисел заменяет собой артикль
entries.position: central determiner in practice — although it is a number, and numbers are normally postdeterminers, zero fills the slot no would fill and admits nothing in front of it: ✗ the zero calories, ✗ my zero absences. It is a cardinal that behaves like a central determiner.
entries.register: neutral in technical and commercial writing; emphatic in speech
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns (zero calories, zero absences) and uncountable nouns (zero tolerance, zero evidence). Not a singular countable noun (✗ zero reason → no reason). The plural is the surprise: every number but one takes a plural noun, so it is zero degrees and 0.5 degrees, not ✗ zero degree. Agreement follows the noun: Zero injuries were reported, but Zero tolerance is the policy.
entries.with of: Rare and best avoided; use none of instead — none of the applicants, not ✗ zero of the applicants (heard informally, but none of is the standard partitive).
entries.pattern: zero [plural noun] · zero [uncountable noun] · zero [noun] for [noun]
entries.contrast: No is the ordinary negative determiner and takes singular countable, plural countable, and uncountable nouns alike (no reason, no reasons, no evidence). Zero is narrower — plural and uncountable only — and carries a technical or emphatic edge: zero tolerance is a policy, no tolerance is a description. For the partitive, none of replaces both.
entries.variants: 0, nil (sports, British), naught/nought, zilch (slang), no (the general negative determiner)
entries.see also: one, none of, a fraction of

entries.meaning: Marks the item that ends a sequence with nothing after it.
examples: The final two episodes were filmed back to back.
This is your final notice before we send the account to collections.
She missed the final deadline by nine minutes.
The judge reserved the final word for herself.
Their final three attempts all failed for the same reason.
We're waiting on final approval from the state.
entries.русский: последний, окончательный — завершающий весь ряд
entries.position: postdeterminer, after a central determiner
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: general ordinal (adjective in the postdeterminer slot)
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns (the final episode), plural countable nouns when a cardinal follows or the set is plural (the final two episodes, the final results), and uncountable nouns in fixed phrases (the final word, final approval).
entries.with of: Takes of only through a noun: the final of the three, the final of the series. Not a partitive determiner on its own.
entries.pattern: the/my/this final [noun] · the final [cardinal] [plural noun] · final [noun] (bare, in fixed compounds: final notice, final approach)
entries.contrast: Final and last overlap, and the difference is definiteness of ending. Final says nothing more will follow, ever — the final episode of a canceled show. Last can simply mean most recent (last week, the last email you sent), which final can never mean. When you want "no more after this," final is unambiguous; last is not.
entries.variants: the very final, the final-ever (informal), ultimate (formal)
entries.see also: last, next, first, remaining

entries.meaning: Ranks an item at position one in a sequence.
examples: The first three chapters are free.
This is my first time flying out of Newark.
She was the first of four children.
First thing tomorrow, call the insurance company.
It was a first attempt, and it showed.
All the first six rows were reserved for family.
entries.pronunciation note: the article in front is weak and takes its consonant form: the first /ðə ˈfɚst/, never ✗ /ði ˈfɚst/
entries.русский: первый — порядковое числительное
entries.position: postdeterminer
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns (the first draft), plural countable nouns when a cardinal or a plural set follows (the first three days, the first responders), and mass nouns naming an instance (the first snow of the season). It normally requires a central determiner in front of it — the, a possessive, or a demonstrative — and is ungrammatical bare before a common noun in most contexts (✗ first draft was rough → the first draft was rough), though it stands bare in fixed phrases (first thing tomorrow, first base, first prize, at first light).
entries.with of: of is required for the partitive: the first of the month, the first of three children, the first of them to arrive.
entries.pattern: the/my/this first [noun] · the first [cardinal] [plural noun] · a first [noun] · the first of [the/my + plural noun] · first [noun] (fixed phrases)
entries.contrast: Ordinal before cardinal. It is the first three chapters, never ✗ the three first chapters — this is the single most common ordering error in the whole determiner system. Note also the first against a first: the first attempt identifies a unique one, a first attempt treats it as one of a possible series (a first attempt at bread). First is also a pronoun — every ordinal is — and it drops the noun rather than the determiner: as a determiner it precedes a noun (the first chapter), as a pronoun it stands alone with the still attached (She was the first to arrive, I'll take the first). Bare first with no the is the adverb (First, sign here).
entries.variants: the very first, first-ever, the first-time (attributive), foremost
entries.see also: second, third, fourth, fifth, last, next, one, former, latter

entries.meaning: Ranks an item at the end of a sequence, or points back to the one immediately before now.
examples: Final in a sequence. The one at the end, with nothing after it.
Most recent. The one immediately before now — this is the article-less use with time nouns.
Least likely. In the last + noun + relative clause: the last person I'd ask.
The last two questions on the exam were the hardest.
I saw her last week at the farmers market.
Sales are up nine percent over the last six months.
He drank the last of the coffee and didn't make more.
She's the last person I'd trust with a secret.
Last night's storm knocked out power on three blocks.
entries.русский: последний; прошлый — во временном значении без артикля: last week — на прошлой неделе
entries.position: postdeterminer; in the time sense it stands alone with no article (last week)
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns (the last chapter, last night), plural countable nouns (the last two weeks, my last three jobs), and uncountable nouns (the last milk in the fridge, the last of the money).
entries.with of: of is required for the partitive: the last of the milk, the last of them, the last of the survivors.
entries.pattern: the/my/this last [noun] · the last [cardinal] [plural noun] · last [time noun] (no article) · the last of [the/my + noun] · the last [noun] to [verb]
entries.contrast: The article changes the meaning, and this is the trap. Last week (bare) means the calendar week before this one; the last week means the most recent seven days, whichever days those are. Same for last year vs. the last year, last month vs. the last month. Never insert a preposition into the bare form: I saw her last week, ✗ in last week. Against final: last can mean merely most recent, final cannot.
entries.variants: the very last, last-minute (attributive), the last but one (penultimate), last but not least
entries.see also: next, final, first, penultimate, second-to-last, next-to-last, previous, prior, preceding, the rest of, the remainder of

examples: Immediately after this one in a sequence. The next flight, the next chapter.
The coming one, counted from now. With time nouns and no article: next week, next summer.
The next three flights to Denver are already full.
I'll call you next Tuesday about the invoice.
The next person who interrupts is leaving.
We spent the next two hours on hold.
Her office is next door to the copy room.
They listed his brother as next of kin.
entries.русский: следующий; будущий — во временном значении без артикля: next week — на следующей неделе
entries.position: postdeterminer; in the time sense it stands alone with no article (next week)
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns (the next flight, next Tuesday) and plural countable nouns (the next three trains, the next few weeks). Not uncountable nouns — a sequence needs discrete items to have a next one, so ✗ the next money, ✗ the next funding, ✗ the next advice. Where the noun is a mass, use the rest of (the rest of the funding) or count it in units (the next round of funding, the next two gallons).
entries.with of: Only in the fixed legal phrase next of kin and in the fused-head partitive, where the noun after of is plural or a number: the next of the three, the next of them. It is not a general partitive determiner — ✗ the next of the milk.
entries.pattern: the next [noun] · the next [cardinal] [plural noun] · next [time noun] (no article) · the next [noun] to [verb] · next door / next of kin
entries.contrast: Mirror image of last, with the same article trap. Next week (bare) is the calendar week after this one; the next week is the seven days from now. And next Tuesday is genuinely ambiguous in American speech — it can mean the Tuesday of this coming week or the Tuesday after that, so name the date if it matters. Against following: next is measured from now, following from some other point already established (the meeting was Monday; the following day she resigned).
entries.variants: the very next, next-day (attributive), next of kin, the next but one
entries.see also: last, subsequent, following, another, final

entries.meaning: Ranks an item at an unspecified high position in a sequence.
examples: For the nth time, the deadline has not moved.
The formula gives you the nth term without computing the ones before it.
He proofreads everything to the nth degree.
This is the umpteenth delay on this project.
She explained it for the umpteenth time and gave up.
That's the zillionth email about the parking lot this week.
entries.русский: энный (тех.); в сотый раз, надцатый (разг., с досадой)
entries.position: postdeterminer, effectively always after the
entries.register: nth is neutral to technical; umpteenth is informal and always exasperated
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns — the nth term, the umpteenth delay. Not plural countable nouns (✗ the umpteenth delays) and not uncountable nouns.
entries.with of: Does not take of.
entries.pattern: the nth [singular noun] · to the nth degree · for the nth/umpteenth time · the umpteenth [singular noun]
entries.contrast: Nth is a real variable in mathematics (the nth term of the series) that has leaked into everyday speech as an intensifier (to the nth degree). Umpteenth has no mathematical life at all — it is purely a complaint, meaning "one more in a series I have lost count of and resent." Zillionth and millionth work the same way informally.
entries.variants: the nth degree, umpteen (the cardinal), zillionth, for the millionth time (hyperbolic)
entries.see also: third, fourth, fifth, penultimate, second-to-last, next-to-last, another, same, umpteen

entries.meaning: Ranks an item by counting backward from the end of a sequence.
examples: The penultimate chapter is the one everybody remembers.
She was sitting in the second-to-last row.
The next-to-last question tripped up half the room.
Stress falls on the penultimate syllable in most Spanish words.
Isn't this the second-to-last box we have to move?
He finished third-to-last and still made the team.
The penultimate of the four movements is the only quiet one.
entries.pronunciation note: the to inside the compounds is weak, /tə/, and is never stressed; the penultimate is /ðə pəˈnʌltəmət/
entries.русский: предпоследний — penultimate книжн., два других обиходные
entries.position: postdeterminer, after the or a possessive
entries.register: penultimate formal and literary; second-to-last and next-to-last are the ordinary American forms
entries.type: general ordinal (counted backward from the end)
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns (the penultimate chapter, the second-to-last row) and plural countable nouns when a cardinal follows (the second-to-last three entries, rare). Not uncountable nouns — ✗ the penultimate money, ✗ the next-to-last evidence — because counting backward, like counting forward, needs discrete items. All three forms normally require the or a possessive: ✗ penultimate chapter bare, though hyphenated attributives appear without one (next-to-last place).
entries.with of: of is required for the partitive: the penultimate of the four movements, the second-to-last of them, the next-to-last of the survivors.
entries.pattern: the penultimate [singular noun] · the second-to-last [singular noun] · the next-to-last [singular noun] · the [ordinal]-to-last [noun] · the penultimate of [the + plural noun]
entries.contrast: The counting runs backward, and it is off by one for most people. Penultimate means second from the end, not "the ultimate, only more so" — that mistaken reading is common enough that plain second-to-last is safer anywhere it matters. Going further back, antepenultimate is third from the end; past that, English gives up and says fourth from the end. Against last: last is one from the end, second-to-last is two from the end. The British the last but one means exactly second-to-last and reads as an import in American prose. Second-to-last and next-to-last are interchangeable in American English; both take hyphens.
entries.variants: antepenultimate (third from the end), the last but one (British), second from the end, third-to-last, the runner-up (of a ranking, a noun rather than a determiner)
entries.see also: last, final, third, fourth, fifth, former, latter, remaining

examples: Rank two in a sequence. The second chapter, the second attempt.
One more of the same kind. With a: a second chance, a second opinion — equivalent to another.
The second witness contradicted the first.
She asked for a second opinion before scheduling surgery.
Nobody wants a second meeting about the same memo.
He was born on the second of March.
They water the plants every second day.
Her second novel sold better than her first.
entries.русский: второй — порядковое числительное
entries.position: postdeterminer
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns (the second draft, a second chance), plural countable nouns when a cardinal follows or the set is inherently plural (the second two rows, second helpings, second thoughts), and uncountable nouns only in fixed phrases (second nature, on second thought). Note that a second helping and second helpings are ordinary countables, not mass nouns — the fixed-phrase exemption covers only the abstract pair.
entries.with of: of is required for the partitive: the second of the month, the second of her three sons.
entries.pattern: the/my/this second [noun] · a second [noun] · the second of [the/my + plural noun] · every second [singular noun] · second [noun] (fixed: second base, second thought)
entries.contrast: The article is a meaning switch. The second chance is chance number two in a numbered series; a second chance just means one more, a synonym of another. A second opinion, a second helping, a second look — all of these are the "additional" sense, not the ranking sense. Note also every second + singular noun, which means alternate ones (every second row), not "each pair."
entries.variants: a second, second-best, second-hand, second to none, every second
entries.see also: first, another, third, fourth, fifth, former, latter

entries.meaning: Ranks an item at position three, four, five, and upward in a sequence.
examples: This is the third time the server has gone down this week.
Her fourth album is the one people actually remember.
He finished fifth out of forty and was thrilled.
The twenty-first floor is mechanical; the elevator skips it.
We meet on the third Thursday of every month.
The ninth juror asked to be excused.
entries.pronunciation note: this is where the switches forms: /ðə/ before a consonant (the third /ðə ˈθɚd/, the fifth /ðə ˈfɪfθ/) but /ði/ before a vowel (the eighth /ði ˈeɪtθ/, the eleventh /ði ɪˈlɛvənθ/). It is never stressed either way.
entries.русский: третий, четвёртый, пятый — порядковые числительные
entries.position: postdeterminer
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns (the third try, the fifth attempt) and plural countable nouns when a cardinal follows or two ordinals are coordinated (the third two weeks, rare; the third and fourth chapters). Not uncountable nouns — ✗ the third water, ✗ the fourth advice; a mass noun has to be counted in units before it can be ranked (the third glass of water, the fourth piece of advice). Like all ordinals it normally requires a central determiner in front of it, and it stands bare only in fixed compounds — third base, third rail, fifth wheel, which are ordinary singular countable nouns rather than exceptions to the rule.
entries.with of: of is required for the partitive: the third of the four defendants, the fifth of July.
entries.pattern: the/my/this [ordinal] [singular noun] · a [ordinal] [singular noun] · the [ordinal] of [the/my + plural noun] · the [ordinal] [noun] to [verb]
entries.contrast: Ordinals still come before cardinals (the third two weeks is legal but odd; the first three weeks is the normal shape). Watch the spelling of the irregulars, which is where most written errors land: first, second, third, fifth (not ✗ fiveth), eighth (one t), ninth (no e), twelfth, twentieth. In compound ordinals only the last element takes the ordinal form: twenty-first, ✗ twentieth-first.
entries.variants: sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth, twelfth, twentieth, twenty-first, hundredth, 3rd / 4th / 5th (numerals)
entries.see also: first, second, two, three, four, a quarter, a third, two-thirds, nth, umpteenth

examples: One more of the same kind. Another cup of coffee, another delay.
A different one. We'll have to find another route.
Give me another minute and I'll have it.
Another three days of rain and the basement floods.
That's yet another reason to leave early.
She's another of his former students.
If this route is closed, we'll take another one.
Another two hundred dollars won't fix the transmission.
Isn't there another way into the building?
He finished his coffee and asked for another.
entries.pronunciation note: the first syllable is the indefinite article, reduced to /ə/ — another is an + other welded together, and the stress never moves onto it (✗ /eɪˈnʌðɚ/)
entries.русский: ещё один; другой — включает в себя артикль an, поэтому другого определителя не терпит
entries.position: central determiner — it contains the indefinite article, which is why nothing else central can join it
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: general ordinal / indefinite determiner (historically an + other)
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns — another chance, another delay. Never an uncountable noun (✗ another information → more information) and never a plural countable noun on its own (✗ another books). The one exception is a quantity phrase, where a plural noun is allowed because the quantity counts as a single unit: another three days, another two hundred dollars, another few minutes, another ten percent.
entries.with of: Required for the partitive, and the noun after of must be plural and determined while the verb stays singular: another of her clients has filed, another of them. ✗ another of client, ✗ another of clients.
entries.pattern: another [singular noun] · another [cardinal] [plural noun] · another of [the/my + plural noun] · another [singular noun] like [noun] · one another
entries.contrast: Another vs. other is the pair to memorize. Another is one word, always singular, and never follows a determiner: ✗ the another day. Other takes a determiner in front of it and works with plurals and uncountables: the other day, other books, other evidence. So a bare singular countable noun requires another, never bare other: ✓ another reason, ✗ other reason. Also distinguish the two senses of another itself — "one more of the same" (another beer) and "a different one" (let's try another route). And note that another is a pronoun as well as a determiner: as a determiner it precedes a noun (another cup), as a pronoun it stands alone (I'll have another, one after another). The verb stays singular either way — Another is on the way.
entries.variants: one another, another one, yet another, a whole nother (informal tmesis, common in American speech; write a whole other)
entries.see also: other, second, next, further, additional, a

entries.meaning: Points back to the first (former) or the second (latter) of two things already mentioned.
examples: Between arbitration and litigation, the former is faster and the latter is more thorough.
The latter two witnesses were never called.
She spent the latter half of her career in public defense.
Her former employer is contesting the unemployment claim.
Of the two routes, the former is scenic and the latter is quick.
The former mayor still keeps an office downtown.
The former testimony was hearsay; the latter evidence was not.
entries.русский: первый (из двух) — последний (из двух); книжн. отсылка к уже названному
entries.position: postdeterminer, effectively always after the
entries.register: formal to neutral; the former … the latter is a writing device more than a speaking one
entries.type: general ordinal (anaphoric — it points back to something already named)
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns (the former proposal, the latter option), plural countable nouns (the latter two candidates, the former tenants), and uncountable nouns when the two things being contrasted are masses (the former evidence was hearsay; the latter testimony was not, the latter funding). Both require the or a possessive in the anaphoric sense — ✗ latter option bare.
entries.with of: of appears in two places, and neither is a partitive on a bare noun. After a quantity noun inside the phrase: the latter half of the year, the former third of the book. And in the fused-head partitive, where former/latter has dropped its noun: the former of the two, the latter of them. Never on the noun itself — ✗ the latter of the option.
entries.pattern: the former [noun] · the latter [noun] · the former … the latter · the latter [cardinal] [plural noun] · her/his former [noun] (the "ex-" sense)
entries.contrast: They work only for exactly two items. With three or more, the latter is wrong — use the last or name the thing. Former has a second life meaning "ex-," and there it does not need a pair: her former employer, the former mayor. Latter has no such second life. Careful readers also object to latter when the two items are far back in the text; if the reader has to hunt, repeat the noun. Both words are determiner and pronoun at once, and in practice the pronoun use is the commoner one: as determiners they precede a noun (the former proposal), as fused-head pronouns they stand alone with the still attached (the former is faster). The verb agrees with what they stand for — The latter is cheaper for one thing, The latter are cheaper for a pair of them.
entries.variants: the latter half, the former of the two, ex- (for the "former" sense), the first … the second
entries.see also: first, last, previous, prior, preceding, subsequent, following

entries.meaning: Adds a quantity to one already in play.
examples: We'll release further details on Monday.
The office is closed until further notice.
Are there any further questions before we vote?
There's an additional charge for checked bags.
They requested additional funding in the spring.
Without further delay, here's the summary.
entries.русский: дополнительный, ещё — further нейтр., additional офиц. и делов.
entries.position: postdeterminer; both appear bare, with no central determiner, before plural and uncountable nouns
entries.register: further is neutral to formal; additional is formal and common in business and legal writing
entries.goes with: further takes uncountable nouns (further information, further delay, further notice) and plural countable nouns (further questions, further cuts); it does not take a bare singular countable noun (✗ further reason → a further reason). Additional takes all three — an additional charge, additional seats, additional funding.
entries.with of: Neither takes of. ✗ further of the information.
entries.pattern: further [uncountable/plural noun] · a further [singular noun] · no further [noun] · additional [noun] · an additional [singular noun] · until further notice
entries.contrast: Further vs. farther is the American split worth keeping: farther for physical distance (three miles farther down the road), further for quantity, degree, and everything abstract — and only further works as a determiner. Further against more: more is the plain comparative of quantity, further adds the idea of continuing something already begun, which is why further discussion implies discussion has already happened and more discussion does not.
entries.variants: no further, until further notice, further to (formal correspondence), extra (informal), supplementary (formal)
entries.see also: another, other, more, remaining

examples: Different from the one named. Some other route, other evidence.
The remaining one or ones of a known set. With the: the other shoe, the other three.
Alternate. In every other + singular noun.
Other airlines charge for the second bag too.
The other two witnesses never testified.
Is there any other evidence you'd like to submit?
I ran into him the other day at the hardware store.
She works from home every other Friday.
We'll need some other explanation for the missing hours.
entries.русский: другой, остальной, прочий — не этот, а иной из того же множества
entries.position: postdeterminer — it follows a central determiner, or stands bare before a plural or uncountable noun
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns (other books, the other two witnesses), uncountable nouns (other evidence, other information), and singular countable nouns only when a determiner precedes it (the other book, my other car, some other reason). It cannot precede a bare singular countable noun: ✗ other book → another book.
entries.with of: Marginal as a determiner. The partitive is built with the pronoun others or with a number: the other of the two, others of his generation (formal). Ordinary usage prefers the others.
entries.pattern: the/my/some/any other [noun] · other [plural noun] · other [uncountable noun] · the other [cardinal] [plural noun] · every other [singular noun] · the other day
entries.contrast: Other vs. another — see another: bare + singular countable requires another, and another never takes a determiner in front of it. Other vs. others — other is the determiner and precedes a noun (the other students), others is the pronoun and stands alone (the others left). Never combine them: ✗ the others students. Note also every other, which means alternate ones (every other week = biweekly), not "all the remaining ones."
entries.variants: others (pronoun), the other day, every other, each other, other than (preposition), otherwise
entries.see also: another, same, remaining, the rest of, the remainder of, every other

entries.meaning: Points to the item that came before the one under discussion.
examples: The previous owner repainted everything beige.
She has two prior convictions for the same offense.
No changes may be made without prior written consent.
See the preceding paragraph for the exact wording.
Both previous attempts failed for the same reason.
Prior experience with the software is helpful but not required.
entries.русский: предыдущий, предшествующий — prior юр./офиц., preceding книжн., о тексте
entries.position: postdeterminer
entries.register: previous neutral; prior formal, legal, and administrative; preceding formal and textual
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns (the previous owner, the preceding paragraph), plural countable nouns (the two previous attempts, prior convictions), and uncountable nouns (prior notice, prior experience, previous employment). Previous and preceding normally need the or a possessive; prior is the one that appears comfortably bare, especially in legal and business phrasing (without prior notice, prior authorization).
entries.with of: None of the three is a partitive determiner. Prior to is a separate item — a formal preposition meaning before (prior to the hearing), and plain before is almost always better.
entries.pattern: the previous [noun] · the [cardinal] previous [plural noun] · prior [uncountable noun] · without prior [noun] · the preceding [noun] · prior to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Previous is the everyday word; preceding means specifically the one immediately before, which is why it belongs to documents (the preceding paragraph, the preceding fiscal year); prior means "already existing beforehand" and is at home in law and paperwork (a prior conviction, no prior experience). Against former: former contrasts two named things, previous just points backward in time. Against last: last week is a fixed calendar unit, the previous week is measured from some other point in the narrative.
entries.variants: prior to, the preceding, the aforementioned (formal), earlier, foregoing (legal)
entries.see also: subsequent, following, last, former, latter, next

entries.meaning: Marks what is left of a set after part of it is gone.
examples: The remaining two seats are in the back row.
We'll split the remaining money three ways.
All remaining applicants will hear back by Friday.
She used her remaining vacation days in December.
The remaining balance is due on the first.
Only three of the remaining twelve sites are still active.
entries.русский: оставшийся — тот, что ещё не израсходован или не назван
entries.position: postdeterminer, normally after the or a possessive
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: general ordinal (participial adjective in the postdeterminer slot)
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns (the remaining two seats, the remaining applicants) and uncountable nouns (the remaining money, the remaining time). A singular countable noun works only when the noun is genuinely unique (the remaining copy). It normally requires a central determiner, though notices and headlines drop it: Remaining seats are limited.
entries.with of: Not a partitive determiner itself. The partitive is the rest of or the remainder of.
entries.pattern: the remaining [plural/uncountable noun] · the remaining [cardinal] [plural noun] · my/our remaining [noun] · remaining [plural noun] (bare, in notices)
entries.contrast: Remaining precedes the noun and modifies it; the rest of and the remainder of are partitive phrases that take of and a determined noun after them. They mean the same thing and differ only in shape: the remaining seats = the rest of the seats. Against other: other means different, remaining means left over.
entries.variants: the remainder, the rest, left over / leftover, outstanding (of balances and tasks)
entries.see also: the rest of, the remainder of, other, further, additional, last

entries.meaning: Marks the noun as identical to one already known, rather than merely similar.
examples: The same problem came up in the last audit.
We ordered from that same restaurant twice in one week.
Her answer was the same as it was in March.
The same two people always volunteer.
They offer same-day shipping on anything ordered before noon.
It's the very same car he drove in high school.
Every lawyer we called gave us the same advice.
entries.русский: тот же самый — требует перед собой the, this или that
entries.position: postdeterminer — it requires a central determiner, nearly always the, this, or that
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: all three noun types — singular countable (the same problem), plural countable (the same two people), and uncountable (the same information, the same advice). What it cannot do is stand bare before a noun in ordinary prose: ✗ same problem came up again → the same problem came up again. It stands bare only in fixed and commercial compounds (same-day shipping, same-sex marriage) and in elliptical replies (Same here, Same to you).
entries.with of: Does not take of. The comparison is made with as (the same as before) or with a relative clause (the same one that broke) — ✗ the same of.
entries.pattern: the same [noun] · this/that same [noun] · the same [noun] as [noun phrase] · the same [cardinal] [plural noun] · the very same [noun] · same-day / same-sex (compound modifiers)
entries.contrast: The same points at identity — one thing, met twice. Similar points at resemblance — two things that are alike. American English uses the same as for the comparison (the same as last year); the same like is not English. Note that the same also works as a pronoun (I'll have the same), and that this same and that same are legal because same is a postdeterminer, so a demonstrative can occupy the central slot in front of it.
entries.variants: the very same, this/that same, one and the same, the selfsame (literary), same old (informal)
entries.see also: other, another, this, former, latter

entries.meaning: Points to the item that comes after the one under discussion.
examples: The following morning she filed the complaint.
Subsequent revisions were minor and mostly cosmetic.
Attendance dropped in each of the subsequent three years.
Please bring the following: a photo ID, proof of address, and the signed form.
The following pages list every exception.
In the ensuing confusion, two boxes went missing.
entries.русский: последующий, следующий — subsequent офиц., юр. и науч.
entries.position: postdeterminer
entries.register: subsequent formal, legal, and academic; following neutral to formal
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns (the following day, the subsequent hearing), plural countable nouns (the subsequent two years, the following pages), and uncountable nouns (subsequent correspondence, subsequent damage). Both normally take the, though subsequent appears bare in formal writing (subsequent revisions were minor).
entries.with of: Neither takes of. Subsequent to is a formal preposition meaning after (subsequent to the merger) and plain after is nearly always better.
entries.pattern: the following [noun] · the subsequent [noun] · the subsequent [cardinal] [plural noun] · subsequent to [noun phrase] · the following: [list]
entries.contrast: Following is measured from a point already established in the text or the narrative (the meeting was Monday; the following day she resigned), while next is measured from now. That is the whole difference, and it is why a report says the following year and a conversation says next year. The following also has a job no other word here has — introducing a list, with a colon: Please bring the following: a photo ID, proof of address, and the signed form.
entries.variants: subsequent to, the following, ensuing, succeeding, thereafter (adverb)
entries.see also: next, previous, prior, preceding, further, additional, last

entries.meaning: The dialect form of the other — of two, the one not just named.
examples: "You take one end and I'll take t'other."
He come by t'other day asking after the mule.
One of 'em was lying and t'other one knew it.
The cabin sits on t'other side of the creek, past the fence line.
It don't matter which — one or t'other will do.
In standard English write the other: t'other day → the other day.
entries.pronunciation note: one word, two syllables, no pause at the apostrophe — the t- is simply the first sound of the word. The commonest weakening in running speech is the whole phrase, not the word: t'other day /ˈtʌðɚ ˈdeɪ/
entries.русский: тот, другой — диал./устар. стяжение the other; аппалачское и южное просторечие
entries.position: central determiner — it has the definite article baked into it, so nothing else central can join it: ✗ the t'other side
entries.register: regional and archaic. In American English it is Appalachian and Southern mountain speech first, older rural speech elsewhere second, and in print it belongs to dialect writing — Twain, Joel Chandler Harris, local-color fiction — and to the fixed pair one … t'other. It is not standard written English, and a reader who knows it hears it as country, not as an error.
entries.type: general ordinal (dialect form of the other)
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns (t'other side, t'other day) and plural countable nouns (t'other ones, t'other two) — the same range as the other. Not uncountable nouns in ordinary dialect use.
entries.with of: Not a partitive determiner. In the fused-head pronoun use it simply stands alone, normally paired against one: one or t'other, each blamed t'other.
entries.pattern: t'other [singular noun] · t'other [plural noun] · one … t'other (paired) · one or t'other · t'other day / t'other side / t'other night
entries.contrast: It is the other, article and all, which is why a second determiner cannot stand in front of it and why standardizing it means dropping the t: t'other day → the other day. The apostrophe is a misreading that history left behind — the t- is a fossil of the old demonstrative that, not a clipped the, and the older spelling is plain tother. The paired frame one … t'other is the dialect equivalent of the one … the other and of the bookish former, latter. For the standard word, see other.
entries.variants: tother (older spelling), tuther (eye dialect), one … t'other, t'other one, the other (standard)
entries.see also: other, another, former, latter, th', the

entries.meaning: Names a large, roughly measured piece of a whole, in conversational register.
examples: A chunk of the budget disappears into insurance every year.
A good chunk of the audience left at intermission.
Rewriting the intake form ate a chunk of my afternoon.
A chunk of the retaining wall came down in the storm.
They still owe us a good chunk of it.
Replacing the transmission is a chunk of change.
entries.pronunciation note: a is weak /ə/ and of reduces to /əv/ or simply /ə/ in fast speech — a chunk of the money is usually /ə ˈtʃʌŋk ə ðə ˈmʌni/
entries.русский: изрядная часть, кусок — разг.: заметная доля чего-либо
entries.position: a is the central determiner of chunk; the whole phrase heads a partitive
entries.register: informal to neutral — conversational American, ordinary in business talk and journalism, out of place in a contract or a specification
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns (a chunk of the budget, a chunk of time) and singular countable nouns naming a divisible whole (a chunk of the retaining wall, a chunk of the afternoon). With plural countable nouns it is marginal — a chunk of the applicants is heard, but a lot of the applicants is better — because chunk divides a mass and does not select from a group.
entries.with of: Required. ✗ a chunk the budget. The noun after of may be bare when it is a mass (a chunk of money, a chunk of change) or determined for the true partitive (a chunk of the budget).
entries.pattern: a chunk of [the/my/this + noun] · a good/big/fair/sizable chunk of [noun phrase] · a chunk of [pronoun] · a chunk of change (fixed, = a lot of money)
entries.contrast: Against a fraction of, which always means small, a chunk of always means big — and a good chunk of means bigger still, close to most of. Against part of, which is neutral about size and at home in formal prose, this one is informal and carries the picture of something bitten out of a whole. Agreement is notional, following the noun after of: A chunk of the money is missing, A chunk of the shipments were late. The fixed a chunk of change means a large sum and is never used of a small one.
entries.variants: a good chunk of, a big chunk of, a fair chunk of, a sizable chunk of, a chunk of change, a hunk of (of solid matter)
entries.see also: a fraction of, part of, the better part of, the bulk of, a bunch of

entries.meaning: Names a small, unspecified share of a whole.
examples: You can get the same coverage at a fraction of the price.
Only a fraction of the applicants made it past the first round.
A fraction of the money ever reached the schools.
The repair took a fraction of the time we budgeted.
A small fraction of users ever change the default settings.
She read a fraction of it and put it down.
entries.русский: малая доля, ничтожная часть — подчёркивает, как мало это от целого
entries.position: a is the central determiner of fraction; the whole phrase heads a partitive
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns (a fraction of the cost), plural countable nouns (a fraction of the applicants), and singular countable nouns naming a divisible whole (a fraction of the building). Not a bare noun: ✗ a fraction of applicants is odd — the noun after of is normally determined.
entries.with of: Required. A fraction cannot precede a noun directly: ✗ a fraction the cost.
entries.pattern: a fraction of [the/my/this + noun] · a fraction of [pronoun] · a small/tiny fraction of [noun phrase] · at a fraction of [the + noun]
entries.contrast: Unlike a third or two-thirds, a fraction of names no specific share — it means "a very small part," and it is always understood as small. So a fraction of the cost is a bargain, while a portion of the cost is neutral about size. Verb agreement is notional: A fraction of the budget was spent, A fraction of the residents were notified.
entries.variants: a small fraction of, a tiny fraction of, a portion of, a percentage of
entries.see also: a quarter, a third, two-thirds, percent, part of, the bulk of

entries.meaning: Names a share of a group or an amount, sized only by whatever adjective is put in front of it.
examples: A large proportion of the respondents skipped the last page.
A small proportion of the funding is restricted to capital projects.
A proportion of every gift goes straight to the endowment.
What proportion of the caseload is housing?
The proportion of first-generation students has risen every year since 2018.
Only a proportion of them will ever renew.
entries.pronunciation note: a /ə/, the first syllable of proportion /prə/, and of /əv/ are all weak; the phrase carries one beat, on -por-
entries.русский: доля, некоторая часть — книжн., науч.: часть от общего числа
entries.position: a is the central determiner of proportion; the whole phrase heads a partitive
entries.register: formal — statistics, research writing, public health, and policy. In ordinary prose a percentage or some of is plainer.
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns (a proportion of the respondents) and uncountable nouns (a proportion of the funding). A singular countable noun only when it names a divisible whole (a proportion of the estate). The noun after of is normally determined.
entries.with of: Required. ✗ a proportion the applicants. Without of, proportion is an ordinary noun about ratio and shape (out of proportion, the proportions of the room) and not a determiner at all.
entries.pattern: a proportion of [the/my/these + noun] · a large/small/significant proportion of [noun phrase] · a proportion of [pronoun] · the proportion of [noun] who/that [verb] · what proportion of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Bare a proportion of says almost nothing — every share is a proportion, so the phrase does no work until an adjective sizes it: a large proportion of, a small proportion of. That is what separates it from a fraction of, which is understood as small on its own, and from the majority of, which is understood as more than half. In plain writing a number says it better: a proportion of respondents → thirty percent of respondents. Note the separate the proportion of, which names the ratio itself rather than a share of a group: The proportion of first-generation students has doubled. Agreement is otherwise notional: A proportion of the funding was withheld, A proportion of the respondents were undecided.
entries.variants: a large proportion of, a small proportion of, a significant proportion of, the proportion of, a percentage of, a share of
entries.see also: a fraction of, percent, the majority of, the minority of, one in three, nine out of ten, a quarter, a third, two-thirds

entries.respell: uh KWOR-tur, uh THURD, too THURDZ
entries.meaning: Names an exact share of a whole.
examples: A third of the class failed the midterm.
Two-thirds of the water in the reservoir evaporated.
She finished in a quarter of the time it took me.
Three-quarters of the respondents said they'd switch.
The new unit is a third the size of the old one.
Wait a quarter of an hour and try the door again.
entries.pronunciation note: the a is weak, /ə/, and so is the of that follows: a third of the class /ə ˈθɚd əv ðə ˈklæs/
entries.русский: четверть, треть, две трети — перед определённой группой требуют of: a third of the cake
entries.position: predeterminer in the fraction series, but not a working predeterminer the way half is. Unlike half, these cannot sit bare in front of a central determiner: ✓ half the cake, ✗ a third the cake. Before a determined noun phrase they take of and head a partitive instead (a third of the cake), and the bare predeterminer use survives only in measure comparisons — a third the size, two-thirds the price.
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns (two-thirds of the water), plural countable nouns (a third of the students), and singular countable nouns naming a divisible whole (a quarter of the pie, a quarter of an hour).
entries.required before a determined noun phrase: two-thirds of the students, ✗ two-thirds the students. Of is optional only before a measure noun in a comparison: a third the size, two-thirds the price, a quarter the weight. Before a pronoun it is required: a third of them.
entries.pattern: a/one third of [the/my/this + noun] · [cardinal]-[ordinal plural] of [noun phrase] · a quarter of [pronoun] · a third [the + measure noun] (comparison) · three-quarters of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Half is the exception in this family — it drops of freely (half the cake) where the others cannot (✗ a third the cake). Hyphenation: hyphenate a fraction used as a modifier and, by American convention, as a noun too — two-thirds, three-quarters, seven-eighths. Agreement is notional: Two-thirds of the budget is gone, Two-thirds of the seats are taken.
entries.variants: a fourth (American alternative to a quarter), three-quarters, five-eighths, one-third (formal/technical), a quarter of an hour
entries.see also: half, percent, a fraction of, third, fourth, fifth

entries.meaning: Takes in every part or every member of a known whole — the totality member of the fractions-and-part-words family. For the word's full entry as a predeterminer, including floating all, see all.
examples: All of the milk had gone sour by Thursday.
All of us were in the parking lot when the alarm went off.
She read all of it twice before signing anything.
All of the applicants who made the second round were local.
Not all of the damage is covered.
All of Ohio was under a wind advisory by noon.
entries.pronunciation note: of is weak, /əv/, and drops to /ə/ before a consonant — all of the money is usually /ˈɔl ə ðə ˈmʌni/, while before a pronoun the /v/ links forward: all of it /ˈɔl əv ɪt/. All itself keeps its full vowel.
entries.русский: все, всё из — весь объём уже определённой группы: all of the students
entries.position: predeterminer all plus of; the phrase heads a partitive over an already-determined noun phrase
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns (all of the students), uncountable nouns (all of the money, all of the time), singular countable nouns naming a divisible whole or a stretch (all of the cake, all of the afternoon), and — the use that makes the of obligatory — pronouns: all of us, all of them, all of it.
entries.optional before a determiner: all (of) the students, all (of) my money, with the of-less form the more common American choice.
entries.required before a pronoun: all of them, ✗ all them (heard in casual and regional speech, not standard).
entries.pattern: all of [the/my/this + noun] · all of [pronoun] · all [the/my + noun] (no of) · all of [proper noun] · not all of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: This is the totality end of the same series as half of and two-thirds of, and it behaves like half in the one way that matters: both may drop of in front of a determiner where the other fractions may not — ✓ all the cake, ✓ half the cake, ✗ a third the cake. Against bare all plus a bare noun, which is generic: all students need an ID is about students in general, all of the students is about a specific known set. Agreement is notional, following the noun after of: All of the cake is gone, All of the cookies are gone.
entries.variants: all the, all my, not all of, the whole of, every one of, all them (nonstandard)
entries.see also: all, half, the whole (of), the rest of, the remainder of, every one of, none of

entries.meaning: Divides a quantity into two equal parts and names one of them.
examples: Half the class failed the midterm.
She spent half of her paycheck on the deposit.
Give me half an hour and I'll have the numbers.
Half of it was still frozen in the middle.
Kids under six ride at half price.
Half the time he doesn't even read the email.
Half the seats were still empty at kickoff.
Didn't half the committee vote against it?
entries.pronunciation note: the l is silent; everything around it reduces — half the cake /ˌhæf ðə ˈkeɪk/, half a dozen /ˌhæf ə ˈdʌzən/, half an hour /ˌhæf ən ˈaʊɚ/, half of it /ˌhæf əv ɪt/
entries.русский: половина, пол- — предопределитель: стоит перед the/my/that (half the cake)
entries.position: predeterminer — it stands ahead of the central determiner (half the cake, half my paycheck, half that amount)
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: all three noun types — singular countable (half the cake, half an hour), plural countable (half the students), and uncountable (half the water, half my time). It also precedes bare nouns in fixed price and time phrases: half price, half fare, half time.
entries.with of: Optional before a determiner: half (of) the cake, half (of) my paycheck — both are standard, and the of-less form is more common in American speech. Required before a pronoun: half of it, half of them, ✗ half them.
entries.pattern: half [the/my/this + noun] · half of [the/my/this + noun] · half of [pronoun] · half a/an [singular noun] · a half [singular noun] · half [bare price/time noun]
entries.contrast: Half is the only fraction that can skip of before a determiner — ✗ a third the cake but ✓ half the cake. On a half hour vs. half an hour: both are standard American English; a half an hour is common in speech but redundant in writing. Agreement is notional, following the noun after half: Half the cake is gone, Half the guests are gone. As a pronoun it stands alone (I'll take half); as a determiner it precedes a noun phrase.
entries.variants: a half, one half, half a, half an, half again, better half, half past, and a half (a year and a half)
entries.see also: a quarter, a third, two-thirds, the whole (of), twice, double, half again as much, all

entries.term: one in three, nine out of ten
entries.respell: WUN in THREE, NYN owt uv TEN
entries.meaning: States a proportion by counting members of a group one at a time — how many out of every so many.
examples: One in three households in the county has no broadband.
Nine out of ten respondents said they would renew.
One out of five prescriptions is never picked up.
One in every eight flights out of the airport was canceled that week.
Roughly one in three of them had been through the program before.
Two out of three voters told pollsters they had already made up their minds.
