entries.pronunciation note: the numbers carry the beats and the joining words reduce — in is /ɪn/ or /ən/, and out of runs together as /ˈaʊɾə/, so nine out of ten dentists is /ˈnaɪn ˈaʊɾə ˈtɛn ˈdɛntɪsts/
entries.русский: каждый третий; девять из десяти — способ выразить долю или частоту
entries.position: the whole frame fills the determiner slot of the noun, or heads a partitive when of follows
entries.register: neutral — the ordinary American way to state a rate in speech, in journalism, and in public-health writing; nine out of ten is also a fixed advertising rhythm
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns — one in three households, nine out of ten dentists. Never an uncountable noun (✗ one in three funding) and never a singular countable noun (✗ one in three household). The noun drops out entirely when it is understood: One in three said no.
entries.with of: The out of frame carries its own fixed of, which is not a partitive: nine out of ten, ✗ nine out ten. A real partitive needs another of and a determined noun — one in three of the households, nine out of ten of them — and before a pronoun it is required: one in three of us.
entries.pattern: one in [cardinal] [plural noun] · [cardinal] out of [cardinal] [plural noun] · one in [cardinal] of [the/my + plural noun] · one in every [cardinal] [plural noun] · [cardinal] in [cardinal] (standing alone)
entries.contrast: Agreement is the trap, and American usage is split. The frame is singular in form and plural in sense, so One in three households is uninsured is the conservative choice, with the verb following one, while One in three households are uninsured is very common and increasingly accepted. Choose one and hold it through a document; the plural reads better when a plural pronoun follows (One in three renters say they…). The two frames mean the same thing (one in three = a third), and the difference from a quarter, a third, two-thirds is rhetorical: a fraction divides a mass, a ratio counts people one at a time, which is why health reporting prefers one in three. Keep the larger number second — ✗ ten out of nine — and do not blend the frames: ✗ nine in out of ten.
entries.variants: one out of five, one out of three, one in ten, two in five, one in every three, a third (the fraction equivalent)
entries.see also: a quarter, a third, two-thirds, percent, a proportion of, a fraction of, the majority of, the minority of

entries.meaning: Names a piece of a single divisible whole.
examples: Part of the problem is that nobody read the contract.
A large part of the budget goes to insurance.
She slept through part of the second act.
Part of the roof came off in the storm.
The delay was in part our fault.
For the most part, the system works.
entries.русский: часть чего-либо — не целиком, а лишь отчасти
entries.position: heads a partitive phrase; part itself takes a, the, or no determiner
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns (part of the problem, part of the money) and singular countable nouns naming a divisible whole (part of the building, part of the movie). Not plural countable nouns — ✗ part of the students → some of the students. That restriction is the entry's whole point: part divides one thing, it does not select from a group.
entries.with of: Required. ✗ part the problem.
entries.pattern: part of [the/my/this + noun] · a part of [noun phrase] · a large/small part of [noun phrase] · part of [pronoun] · in part · for the most part
entries.contrast: Against some of: part of divides a single whole, some of selects members from a plural set — part of the cake but some of the cookies. Against the rest of: part of names a piece, the rest of names everything else. A part of and part of are both fine; the article slightly emphasizes that it is one identifiable piece.
entries.variants: a part of, a large part of, in part, for the most part, a portion of, part and parcel
entries.see also: a fraction of, the rest of, the remainder of, the whole (of), the bulk of, half

entries.meaning: Names a share of a whole expressed in hundredths.
examples: Ten percent of the class dropped before the deadline.
Nearly forty percent of the budget goes to salaries.
They're offering a fifteen percent discount through Sunday.
Two percent of respondents had never heard of the company.
Turnout rose by three percentage points, not three percent.
About ninety percent of it is recyclable.
entries.русский: процент — после числа без -s: ten percent
entries.position: postdeterminer inside the quantity phrase; the whole phrase heads a partitive
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns (ten percent of the budget) and plural countable nouns (ten percent of the students) through of. Directly before a noun it appears only as a hyphen-free attributive quantity: a 10 percent raise, a two percent decline.
entries.with of: Required before a determined noun phrase or a pronoun: ten percent of the vote, ten percent of them. ✗ ten percent the vote.
entries.pattern: [number] percent of [the/my/this + noun] · [number] percent of [pronoun] · a [number] percent [noun] (attributive) · [number] percent (standing alone)
entries.contrast: It never takes -s: ten percent, ✗ ten percents. (The noun percentage is the one that pluralizes: percentages.) American English writes it as one word, percent; British English writes per cent. Agreement is notional — Ten percent of the budget was cut, Ten percent of the students were absent. And keep percent apart from percentage point: a rate that moves from 4% to 5% has risen one percentage point but twenty-five percent.
entries.variants: per cent (British), %, percentage of, percentage point, basis point (finance)
entries.see also: a quarter, a third, two-thirds, a fraction of, the majority of, the minority of, hundred, thousand, million, billion

entries.meaning: Names the sum of a set of separate amounts, taken together as one figure.
examples: The aggregate of the monthly payments exceeds the purchase price by a third.
Coverage is capped at the aggregate of all claims filed in the policy year.
The aggregate of the fines came to just under nine thousand dollars.
Taken in the aggregate, the returns look better than any single quarter does.
The aggregate of the outstanding indebtedness is disclosed in Note 7.
In plain English, the aggregate of the payments is the payments added up.
entries.pronunciation note: the article switches form: the is /ði/ before the vowel of aggregate, never ✗ /ðə/. The noun's last syllable is a schwa, /-ɡət/, where the verb aggregate ends /-ɡeɪt/; of is weak, /əv/.
entries.русский: совокупность, общая сумма — юр., фин. и страховой термин
entries.position: heads a partitive phrase; the is fixed in front of it
entries.register: legal, financial, and technical — insurance policies, contracts, and accounting, where the aggregate is a defined term. In ordinary prose the total of or plain all says it.
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns (the aggregate of the payments, the aggregate of all claims) and uncountable nouns naming an amount (the aggregate of the indebtedness). Not a singular countable noun unless it names a divisible whole.
entries.with of: Required, and the is required in front: ✗ aggregate of the payments, ✗ the aggregate the payments. Without of, in the aggregate is a fixed adverbial meaning "taken all together," and aggregate standing before a noun is an adjective (the aggregate limit, aggregate demand), not a determiner.
entries.pattern: the aggregate of [the/all + plural noun] · the aggregate of [the + uncountable amount noun] · an aggregate of [number] · in the aggregate · aggregate [noun] (adjective)
entries.contrast: Against the totality of, which insists nothing was left out, the aggregate of insists the parts were added up — it is a sum, not a whole. Against a total of, which introduces a figure in a news report, this one introduces a noun phrase in a contract: a total of forty-one claims against the aggregate of all claims. The technical sense is worth knowing because it costs money — an insurance policy's aggregate limit caps everything paid in a policy period, where the per-occurrence limit caps a single claim. Agreement follows aggregate and stays singular: The aggregate of the payments exceeds the cap.
entries.variants: in the aggregate, an aggregate of, aggregate limit (insurance), the sum of, the total of, the whole of
entries.see also: the totality of, a total of, the bulk of, the whole (of), all of

entries.meaning: Names most of a span or an amount — usually a stretch of time, usually with a note of impatience.
examples: We spent the better part of an hour on hold with the insurance company.
She's been at that firm the better part of a decade.
Rewiring the panel took the better part of two days.
The better part of the shipment was still sitting in Newark on Friday.
He drank the better part of a pot of coffee before nine.
It rained the better part of the week we were there.
entries.pronunciation note: the is /ðə/ before the consonant and of is weak /əv/; the tt of better is a flap, /ˈbɛɾɚ/, so the phrase runs together as /ðə ˈbɛɾɚ ˈpɑrɾ əv/
entries.русский: бо́льшая часть, добрых — почти весь: добрых два часа, и всё впустую
entries.position: heads a partitive phrase; the is fixed in front of it
entries.register: neutral to informal — conversational and journalistic, and it carries a faint complaint: the time went and there is nothing to show for it
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns and singular countable nouns naming a span, above all spans of time — the better part of an hour, the better part of a decade, the better part of the afternoon, the better part of a tank of gas. With plural countable nouns it is unidiomatic: ✗ the better part of the applicants → most of the applicants.
entries.with of: Required, and the is required in front: ✗ better part of an hour, ✗ the better part an hour.
entries.pattern: the better part of [a/an + time noun] · the better part of [the + uncountable noun] · the better part of [a + measure noun] · the best part of [noun phrase] (British)
entries.contrast: It means most of, nearly all of — not "the superior half." The better part of an hour is fifty minutes, not thirty. Against the bulk of and most of, which are neutral and handle counts of people and things, this one is idiomatic, wants a span rather than a set, and implies the span was wearing: We spent the better part of a week on hold. The British the best part of means exactly the same and reads as an import. Do not confuse it with the unrelated discretion is the better part of valor, where better part means the wiser portion. Agreement is normally singular, since the noun after of is normally a mass or a stretch: The better part of the afternoon was gone.
entries.variants: the best part of (British), most of, the bulk of, the greater part of, nearly all of
entries.see also: the bulk of, a chunk of, most, the majority of, the minority of, half

entries.meaning: Names the largest share of something, viewed as mass rather than as a count.
examples: The bulk of the work happens in the first two weeks.
The bulk of the settlement went to legal fees.
She wrote the bulk of it on a plane.
The bulk of the shipment is still sitting in Newark.
The bulk of the applicants never finished the second form.
The bulk of our revenue comes from three clients.
entries.русский: основная масса, львиная доля — подавляющая часть
entries.position: heads a partitive phrase; the is fixed
entries.register: neutral to formal; common in journalism and business writing
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns (the bulk of the work, the bulk of the money) and plural countable nouns (the bulk of the applicants). Not a singular countable noun unless it names a divisible mass (the bulk of the shipment).
entries.with of: Required, and the is required in front: ✗ bulk of the work, ✗ the bulk the work.
entries.pattern: the bulk of [the/my/this + noun] · the bulk of [pronoun] · the bulk of [possessive + noun]
entries.contrast: The bulk of and the majority of both mean "most," but the bulk of prefers mass and volume (the bulk of the funding) while the majority of prefers countable sets and is the only one at home with people and votes (the majority of voters). Plain most of covers both and is shorter — the bulk of earns its keep mainly when the writer wants weight and heft in the sentence. Agreement is notional: The bulk of the work is done, The bulk of the applicants were rejected.
entries.variants: most of, the greater part of, the lion's share of, the preponderance of (formal)
entries.see also: the majority of, the minority of, part of, most, the rest of, the remainder of

entries.term: the majority of, the minority of
entries.respell: thuh muh-JOR-uh-tee uv, thuh muh-NOR-uh-tee uv
entries.meaning: Names the larger (majority) or smaller (minority) share of a countable group.
examples: The majority of voters were still undecided a week out.
A majority of the committee voted to postpone.
The vast majority of complaints concern one department.
Only a small minority of users ever contact support.
The majority of them had never flown before.
In the minority of cases where it fails, the fix is manual.
entries.русский: большинство — меньшинство (из чего-либо)
entries.position: heads a partitive phrase
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns first and foremost — the majority of voters, the majority of the applicants. With uncountable nouns it is awkward at best (✗ the majority of the water → most of the water), which is the trap: reach for most of whenever the noun is a mass.
entries.with of: Required before a noun phrase or pronoun: the majority of them. Majority can also stand alone as a noun with no of (The majority ruled), and in that use it is not a determiner.
entries.pattern: the majority of [the/my/these + plural noun] · a majority of [plural noun] · the vast majority of [plural noun] · the majority of [pronoun] · a small minority of [plural noun]
entries.contrast: A majority vs. the majority. A majority is a counting fact — more than half, the winning side of a vote. The majority is the greater part of a known group, closer to most. Agreement follows the noun after of: The majority of voters were undecided (plural), but The majority was decisive when majority stands alone as a single body. Prefer most of with mass nouns and in plain prose.
entries.variants: a majority, the vast majority of, the overwhelming majority of, a small minority of, most of
entries.see also: the bulk of, percent, most, a fraction of

entries.term: the rest of, the remainder of
entries.respell: thuh REST uv, thuh rih-MAYN-dur uv
entries.meaning: Names everything left over once a part has been taken out.
examples: The rest of the milk had gone sour.
He spent the rest of the afternoon on hold.
The rest of us waited in the parking lot.
The remainder of the balance is due within thirty days.
Take what you need and leave the rest of it.
The rest of the questions were multiple choice.
entries.русский: остальное, остаток — remainder книжн., фин. и мат.
entries.position: heads a partitive phrase; the is fixed
entries.register: the rest of neutral; the remainder of formal, financial, and mathematical
entries.goes with: all three noun types — singular countable (the rest of the cake), plural countable (the rest of the cookies), and uncountable (the rest of the money, the rest of the time).
entries.with of: Required before any noun phrase or pronoun: the rest of us, the rest of the day. Without of, the rest is a pronoun standing alone: You take these; I'll handle the rest.
entries.pattern: the rest of [the/my/this + noun] · the rest of [pronoun] · the remainder of [noun phrase] · the rest (pronoun, standing alone)
entries.contrast: The rest of names everything not already accounted for — it is the complement of whatever share you just mentioned. The remaining does the same work as a premodifier with no of: the remaining seats = the rest of the seats. The remainder of is the formal twin of the rest of, and in arithmetic it has a technical meaning (what is left after division) that the rest does not. Agreement is notional: The rest of the cake is gone, The rest of the cookies are gone.
entries.variants: the remainder, the rest, what's left of, the balance of (financial), the residue of (legal)
entries.see also: remaining, part of, the bulk of, other, half

entries.meaning: Names everything in a set considered together as one indivisible whole.
examples: The court reviews the totality of the circumstances, not any single factor.
The totality of the evidence points one direction.
Officers may consider the totality of what they observed at the scene.
The totality of his holdings came out only after the audit.
The report has to be read in its totality to make any sense.
In plain English, the totality of the evidence is all the evidence.
entries.pronunciation note: the is /ðə/ and of is weak /əv/; the t between vowels inside totality is a flap, /toʊˈtæləɾi/
entries.русский: вся совокупность, всё в целом — юр. и книжн.; ср. «по совокупности обстоятельств»
entries.position: heads a partitive phrase; the is fixed in front of it
entries.register: formal, legal, and academic. In American law it is a term of art — the totality of the circumstances is the standard a court applies when no single factor decides the question. Outside that world it is a heavy way to say all of.
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns (the totality of the circumstances, the totality of his holdings) and uncountable nouns (the totality of the evidence, the totality of human knowledge). A singular countable noun only when it names a whole system or record (the totality of the record).
entries.with of: Required, and the is required in front: ✗ totality of the evidence, ✗ the totality the evidence. The one of-less use is the adverbial in its totality.
entries.pattern: the totality of [the + plural noun] · the totality of [the + uncountable noun] · the totality of the circumstances (legal standard) · in its totality
entries.contrast: Against all of, the plain everyday form, the totality of insists on the whole considered as one thing — which is the legal point of the totality of the circumstances: no single fact controls, the court weighs them together. Against the aggregate of, which adds separate amounts into a sum, this one gathers items into a whole with no arithmetic. Against the whole (of), which is ordinary English and prefers a singular noun, this is formal and prefers a plural or a mass. In plain writing, the totality of the evidence is all the evidence. Agreement stays singular, following totality: The totality of the circumstances supports the stop.
entries.variants: in its totality, the totality of the circumstances (legal), the entirety of, the whole of, all of
entries.see also: the whole (of), all of, the aggregate of, the rest of, the remainder of, all

entries.meaning: Names something in its entirety, with no part of it missing or left out. This entry covers whole as the totality member of the fractions-and-part-words family — the complement of half, part of, and the rest of. For the word's full entry as a general postdeterminer, see whole.
examples: Tell me the whole story, not the version you gave the police.
She waited a whole hour and then left without saying anything.
My whole family showed up unannounced on a Tuesday.
He spent the whole afternoon on hold with the insurance company.
The whole of Europe was watching the vote.
It rained the whole three days we were there.
entries.русский: весь, целиком — требует определителя перед собой: the whole day, my whole life
entries.position: postdeterminer — it requires a central determiner in front of it (the whole, a whole, my whole)
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns (the whole story, a whole hour, my whole life, the whole afternoon) and uncountable nouns (the whole truth, the whole point, my whole attention). Never a plural countable noun in this sense — ✗ the whole students → all the students. It does precede a plural noun when a cardinal comes between them, because the number makes the stretch one unit: the whole three days. The plural whole grains, whole numbers, whole milk is a different word — a plain adjective meaning "undivided," not a determiner.
entries.with of: Optional and formal before a determined noun phrase: the whole of the morning, the whole of Europe — the bare the whole morning is the American default. Required before a pronoun: the whole of it, though all of it is the more idiomatic American choice.
entries.pattern: the whole [singular/uncountable noun] · a whole [singular noun] · my/his/their whole [noun] · the whole [cardinal] [plural noun] · the whole of [the + noun] · the whole of [pronoun]
entries.contrast: Whole and all split the work by noun type and by position. Whole is a postdeterminer and takes a singular noun (the whole cake, my whole life); all is a predeterminer and takes plural and uncountable nouns, standing in front of the determiner (all the cakes, all my life). Where both are possible they mean different things: the whole cake is one cake with nothing missing, all the cake is however much cake there happens to be. Whole is also the complement of half and part of — it insists nothing was left out.
entries.variants: a whole, the whole of, the whole thing, a whole nother (informal, for a whole other), entire (formal), wholly (adverb)
entries.see also: whole, half, part of, the rest of, the remainder of, all, every

entries.meaning: Multiplies a quantity by a stated number, from outside the noun phrase rather than inside it.
examples: Processing time dropped by a factor of four after the rewrite.
The original estimate was off by a factor of ten.
Rents in that corridor have risen by a factor of three since 2010.
Their error rate is lower by a factor of two, which is less impressive than it sounds.
Reducing the dose by a factor of five is not the same as reducing it by five.
✗ It costs a factor of three the original price. → ✓ It costs three times the original price.
entries.pronunciation note: a /ə/ and of /əv/ are both weak; the beats fall on fac- and on the number — by a factor of ten is /baɪ ə ˈfæktɚ əv ˈtɛn/, with by unstressed too
entries.русский: во столько-то раз — тех.: by a factor of ten — в десять раз
entries.position: never in a determiner slot; it is the object of by and modifies a verb or a comparison, not a noun
entries.register: technical, scientific, financial, and journalistic — the register of reports rather than conversation
entries.goes with: nothing, as a determiner. It attaches to a number inside the fixed frame by a factor of + [cardinal] and reports how much something grew, shrank, or missed: rose by a factor of ten, off by a factor of two. It never precedes a noun: ✗ a factor of ten the price, ✗ a factor of ten people.
entries.with of: The of is required and fixed — part of the phrase, not a partitive: by a factor of three, ✗ by a factor three.
entries.pattern: [verb] by a factor of [cardinal] · off by a factor of [cardinal] · [comparative] by a factor of [cardinal] · a factor of [cardinal] higher/lower/faster
entries.contrast: This entry exists to block an error. Double, triple, and three times are predeterminers that stand in front of a noun phrase (triple the price); a factor of cannot — it multiplies a verb or a comparison, never a noun. So ✓ The cost rose by a factor of three and ✓ three times the cost, but ✗ a factor of three the cost. Watch the arithmetic that comes with the word: by a factor of ten means ten times as large, and reduced by a factor of ten means down to a tenth, not down by a tenth — which is why careful writing says to one-tenth. Compare an order of magnitude, the same idea locked to powers of ten.
entries.variants: by a factor of, an order of magnitude, X times, X-fold, times over
entries.see also: three times, an order of magnitude, twofold, threefold, tenfold, double, percent

entries.meaning: Multiplies or divides a quantity by a power of ten, from outside the noun phrase.
examples: Solar has gotten an order of magnitude cheaper since 2010.
The new index is orders of magnitude faster on the same hardware.
Their estimate and ours differ by an order of magnitude.
Two orders of magnitude is a hundredfold, not twice.
The risk is an order of magnitude higher in that age group.
✗ an order of magnitude the cost → ✓ ten times the cost.
entries.pronunciation note: an /ən/ and of /əv/ are weak, so the run in front of the comparative flattens to /ənˈɔrdɚəv/; the beats fall on or- and mag-
entries.русский: порядок величины — науч./тех.: разница в десять раз
entries.position: never in a determiner slot; it modifies a comparative adjective or adverb (an order of magnitude cheaper) or follows by (grew by an order of magnitude)
entries.register: technical and scientific first, then business and journalism; in conversation ten times says it without the lab coat
entries.type: multiplier phrase (= a power of ten) — not a determiner
entries.goes with: nothing, as a determiner. It attaches to a comparative (an order of magnitude larger, orders of magnitude faster) or to a verb of change through by (fell by an order of magnitude). It never precedes a noun: ✗ an order of magnitude the price, ✗ an order of magnitude people.
entries.with of: Both ofs are fixed parts of the phrase and neither is a partitive: an order of magnitude, ✗ an order magnitude, ✗ an order of the magnitude.
entries.pattern: an order of magnitude [comparative adjective/adverb] · [verb] by an order of magnitude · orders of magnitude [comparative] · two orders of magnitude (= a hundred times) · within an order of magnitude of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: One order of magnitude is a factor of ten, two is a hundred, three is a thousand — the count is of powers of ten, not of multiples, and that is where the phrase gets misused: two orders of magnitude is a hundredfold, not twofold. The bare plural orders of magnitude faster means "very much faster" and is honest hyperbole in speech, dishonest in a specification. Against a factor of, which takes any number at all: by a factor of three is available where an order of magnitude is not, since this one comes only in tens. And like a factor of, it is not a predeterminer — three times and double stand in front of a noun phrase, this cannot.
entries.variants: orders of magnitude, by an order of magnitude, a factor of ten, tenfold, ten times
entries.see also: a factor of, three times, twofold, threefold, tenfold, hundred, thousand, million, billion, percent

entries.meaning: Multiplies the following quantity by two.
examples: They charged us double the advertised price.
The new pump moves double the water in half the time.
She's making double what she made at her last job.
Double the number of applicants showed up.
Take double that dosage only if the doctor says so.
The storm dropped double the normal rainfall for March.
entries.pronunciation note: the central determiner it stands in front of stays weak: double the price /ˈdʌbəl ðə ˈpraɪs/, double an ordinary dose /ˈdʌbəl ən ˈɔrdənɛri ˈdoʊs/
entries.русский: вдвое больше, двойной — предопределитель: double the price — вдвое дороже
entries.position: predeterminer, ahead of the central determiner
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: an already-determined noun phrase naming an amount — double the price, double that dosage, double my usual order. It does not attach to a bare noun as a multiplier: double price is not the multiplier use, and phrases like a double room, double doors, double vision are the adjective, not the determiner.
entries.with of: Never. ✗ double of the price. The one of that appears is inside the noun phrase that follows: double the number of applicants.
entries.pattern: double [the/my/this/that + noun] · double the number of [plural noun] · double [the + measure noun] · a double [noun] (adjective, different word class)
entries.contrast: Double and twice mean the same multiplication and differ in shape. Double attaches to a noun phrase (double the price); twice does that too (twice the price) but is also the one that works before as: twice as expensive, ✗ double as expensive. For comparisons with an adjective, use twice; for a plain doubled amount, either. Double additionally lives as an adjective (a double bed), a verb (prices doubled), and a noun (a stunt double) — only the predeterminer use belongs in this file.
entries.variants: twice, twofold, two times, double the amount, doubly (adverb)
entries.see also: twice, triple, quadruple, three times, half, twofold, threefold, tenfold

entries.meaning: Increases a quantity by fifty percent.
examples: The new lease costs half again as much as the old one.
They hired half again as many seasonal workers this year.
The second engine is half again as powerful.
It took half again as much time as we budgeted.
She sold half again as many units in the fourth quarter.
The premium version holds half again the charge.
entries.русский: в полтора раза больше — амер., разг.
entries.position: predeterminer phrase; the as … as frame carries the comparison
entries.register: neutral to informal; distinctly American
entries.goes with: as much takes uncountable nouns (half again as much money); as many takes plural countable nouns (half again as many people). Choose the one that matches the noun — this is the much/many split, imported whole.
entries.with of: No of. The second half of the frame is as + a noun phrase: half again as much money as last year.
entries.pattern: half again as much [uncountable noun] · half again as many [plural noun] · half again as [adjective] · half again [the + noun] · [verb] half again as much
entries.contrast: It means one and a half times, not "half as much again more" and not "twice." The British form is half as much again, which means exactly the same thing and confuses American readers just as much in reverse. Because both are misread often, technical writing should say one and a half times or fifty percent more and be done with it.
entries.variants: half as much again (British), one and a half times, fifty percent more, half again as many
entries.see also: twice, double, half, three times, much, many

entries.meaning: Names a single occurrence or a rate of one per period. It is not the "one times" member of the multiplier series.
examples: The committee meets once a month.
Water the plant once every ten days.
I only asked once.
She rewrote the opening once more and stopped.
Take the pills once daily with food.
✗ It costs once the price of the original. → ✓ It costs the same as the original.
entries.pronunciation note: the article in the frequency frame is weak and unstressed: once a week /ˈwʌns ə ˈwik/, once an hour /ˈwʌns ən ˈaʊɚ/
entries.русский: (один) раз, однажды — наречие частотности, а не определитель
entries.position: adverbial; it does not occupy a determiner slot before a noun phrase
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: frequency adverb — not a multiplier determiner
entries.goes with: nothing, as a determiner. It heads a frequency phrase with a/an or every (once a week, once every three days) and works as a plain adverb of time (I met him once).
entries.with of: Does not take of.
entries.pattern: once a/an [time noun] · once every [cardinal] [plural time noun] · once [adverbial] · at once · once [clause] (conjunction — a separate word)
entries.contrast: This entry exists to block an error. Twice and three times are multipliers that precede a noun phrase (twice the price, three times the price), and learners reasonably extend the pattern down to once — but ✗ once the price is not English. For a one-times comparison, say the same price or equal to the price. Once keeps only the frequency sense (once a week) and the time-adverb sense (we met once). It is also a subordinating conjunction (once you sign, it's final), which lives with the conjunctions.
entries.variants: at once, once more, once again, once in a while, once upon a time
entries.see also: twice, three times, one, double

entries.meaning: States a rate by naming the unit it is measured against: so much for every one of these.
examples: The lot charges four dollars per hour after the first two.
Output is measured in gallons per minute.
Reimbursement is capped at sixty-five dollars per diem.
The state spends about twelve thousand dollars per student.
Earnings came to $1.42 per share.
In speech it's sixty miles an hour; on the gauge it's miles per hour.
entries.pronunciation note: unstressed and reduced in ordinary use — ten dollars per hour is /ˈtɛn ˈdɑlɚz pɚ ˈaʊɚ/. The full /pɝ/ shows up only under contrastive stress and in the Latin tags per se /pɚ ˈseɪ/ and per diem /pɚ ˈdiəm/.
entries.русский: за, на, в — предлог нормы: per hour — в час; тех. и коммерч. регистр
entries.position: heads a prepositional phrase after a quantity; it fills no determiner slot, and it allows no determiner after it
entries.register: technical and commercial — invoices, contracts, science, and specifications. In speech and ordinary prose the article does this job: sixty miles an hour, not per hour, unless you are reading a gauge.
entries.type: preposition (distributive rate marker) — not a determiner
entries.goes with: a bare singular unit noun of time, weight, distance, volume, or head count — per hour, per pound, per mile, per person, per unit, per share, per capita. It takes no determiner at all, and that is the rule worth memorizing: ✗ per an hour, ✗ per the hour, ✗ per each person. Never a plural (✗ per hours) and never a mass noun (✗ per water → per gallon).
entries.with of: Does not take of.
entries.pattern: [amount] per [bare unit noun] · [number] per [bare unit noun] · per capita / per diem / per annum / per se (Latin) · as per [noun phrase] (business jargon) · per [noun phrase] (= according to)
entries.contrast: Per and the distributive a/an are one job in two registers. Six dollars a pound and six dollars per pound mean exactly the same thing; the first belongs in speech and the second on the invoice — see a (per). The hard rule is that per refuses an article: $22 an hour or $22 per hour, never ✗ $22 per an hour. Against each, which follows the noun and prices items rather than stating a rate (Tickets are $12 each), and against by the, which names the unit a thing is sold or paid in (sold by the pound, paid by the hour). Two business habits draw complaints: as per your request (write as you requested) and per meaning "according to" (per the contract), which is fine in a memo and stiff anywhere else.
entries.variants: a / an (the spoken form), per capita, per diem, per annum, per se, as per, each, by the
entries.see also: a (per), once, twice, each, percent

entries.meaning: Multiplies the following quantity by a stated number.
examples: The house sold for three times what they paid for it.
This model uses four times the electricity of the older one.
Ten times as many people showed up as we planned for.
She earns three times my salary and works fewer hours.
The storm dumped five times the normal rainfall.
It's three times as expensive in the airport shop.
entries.pronunciation note: the determiner behind it never takes stress: three times the price /ˈθri ˌtaɪmz ðə ˈpraɪs/
entries.русский: в три раза, втрое — предопределитель: three times the price
entries.position: predeterminer
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: an already-determined noun phrase naming an amount — three times the price, four times my salary, ten times that number. Also used before as many + plural countable and as much + uncountable: three times as many applicants, three times as much water.
entries.with of: Never. ✗ three times of the price. Any of belongs to the noun phrase inside: three times the number of complaints.
entries.pattern: [cardinal] times [the/my/that + noun] · [cardinal] times as many [plural noun] · [cardinal] times as much [uncountable noun] · [cardinal] times as [adjective] · [cardinal] times the number of [plural noun]
entries.contrast: Times stays plural from three up — three times, ten times — while twice replaces ✗ two times in idiomatic usage (two times the price is grammatical but reads as arithmetic; twice the price is what people say). Below that, once is not a multiplier at all. Match as many to countables and as much to uncountables, exactly as with many and much.
entries.variants: four times, ten times, n times, twice (for two), threefold, X times over
entries.see also: twice, double, triple, quadruple, once, many

entries.meaning: Multiplies the following quantity by three, four, and upward.
examples: The clinic ordered triple the usual supply.
Rebuilding it now would cost quadruple the original estimate.
They're seeing triple the traffic they saw last spring.
The recipe calls for triple the amount of garlic, which is correct.
Quadruple the dose is dangerous, not merely ineffective.
He wants triple what the car is worth.
entries.русский: тройной, втрое; четверной, вчетверо — quadruple и выше книжн. или тех.
entries.position: predeterminer
entries.register: neutral; quadruple and above are formal or technical
entries.goes with: an already-determined noun phrase naming an amount — triple the amount, quadruple the dose. As with double, the attributive adjective is a different word class: a triple play, triple glazing.
entries.with of: Never. ✗ triple of the amount.
entries.pattern: triple [the/my/that + noun] · quadruple [the + noun] · triple the number of [plural noun] · a triple [noun] (adjective)
entries.contrast: After double, American English increasingly prefers the n times form: triple the price is fine, but quadruple the price already sounds like a lab report, and quintuple and sextuple are effectively technical only. Above two, three times, four times, and five times are the natural everyday multipliers. Note that triple and quadruple are also verbs (enrollment tripled) and adjectives (a triple bypass).
entries.variants: treble (British), quintuple, sextuple, threefold, fourfold, three times, four times
entries.see also: double, three times, twofold, threefold, tenfold, twice

entries.meaning: Multiplies the following quantity by two, or names a rate of two per period.
examples: The storm dropped twice the normal rainfall.
They pay twice what the job is worth, and still can't fill it.
There were twice as many people as chairs.
It uses twice as much electricity as the old unit.
The board meets twice a year.
This one is twice as heavy but half the price.
entries.pronunciation note: whatever follows stays weak: twice the price /ˌtwaɪs ðə ˈpraɪs/, twice a year /ˌtwaɪs ə ˈjɪr/, twice as much /ˌtwaɪs əz ˈmʌtʃ/
entries.русский: вдвое; дважды — предопределитель: twice the size — вдвое больше
entries.position: predeterminer, ahead of the central determiner
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: an already-determined noun phrase naming an amount — twice the price, twice that amount, twice my weight. Also twice as many + plural countable, twice as much + uncountable, and twice a/an + time noun in the frequency sense (twice a week).
entries.with of: Never. ✗ twice of the price.
entries.pattern: twice [the/my/that + noun] · twice as many [plural noun] · twice as much [uncountable noun] · twice as [adjective] · twice a/an [time noun] · twice the number of [plural noun]
entries.contrast: Twice and double both multiply by two; twice is the one that also fits the as … as frame (twice as expensive, not ✗ double as expensive) and the frequency frame (twice a week, not ✗ double a week). Two times is grammatical but unidiomatic where twice will do. And once does not join this series before a noun phrase — see once.
entries.variants: two times, double, twofold, twice over, twice as many/much
entries.see also: double, three times, once, half again as much, half

entries.meaning: Expresses multiplication as a property of a change rather than as a determiner on a noun.
examples: The company reported a tenfold increase in support tickets.
Enrollment rose threefold between 2015 and 2020.
The risk is roughly twofold higher in that age group.
Our purpose here is twofold: to explain and to warn.
A hundredfold return is a fantasy, not a forecast.
Costs grew fourfold while revenue stayed flat.
entries.русский: двукратный, трёхкратный, десятикратный — книжн.; rose tenfold — вырос в десять раз
entries.position: attributive adjective inside the noun phrase, after the determiner (a tenfold increase), or a bare adverb after the verb (rose tenfold)
entries.register: formal; the register of reports, science writing, and business news
entries.type: multiplier (adjective before a noun, adverb after a verb) — not a determiner
entries.goes with: as an adjective, singular and plural countable nouns naming a change — a twofold increase, threefold gains. It does not attach to an ordinary noun: ✗ tenfold people, ✗ a tenfold price — the noun has to name growth, a rise, a risk, or a difference.
entries.with of: Does not take of.
entries.pattern: a [n]fold [increase/rise/jump/difference] · [verb] [n]fold · a twofold [problem/purpose] (the "having two parts" sense)
entries.contrast: Unlike double and twice, these never stand in the determiner slot — you cannot say ✗ tenfold the price, only ten times the price or a tenfold increase in price. Twofold has a second sense that has nothing to do with multiplication: "having two parts" (the purpose is twofold), and that sense is far more common than the arithmetic one. Note that a tenfold increase means the amount became ten times as large, not eleven times.
entries.variants: manifold (literary), hundredfold, a twofold purpose, n-fold (technical)
entries.see also: double, three times, triple, quadruple, percent

entries.term: a good, a solid, an easy, a full
entries.respell: uh GUUD, uh SAH-lid, un EE-zee, uh FUUL
entries.meaning: Marks a number as a floor rather than an estimate: this much, if not more.
examples: It's a good twenty miles from here to the interstate.
We waited a solid three hours before anyone came out.
There were an easy two hundred people in the lobby.
She's been at it a full two weeks without a day off.
A good half of them never responded.
That'll take a solid forty minutes in this traffic.
entries.русский: добрых, целых, никак не меньше — усиление минимума: a good twenty miles
entries.position: a/an is the central determiner; the adjective premodifies the cardinal in the postdeterminer slot
entries.register: informal to neutral
entries.goes with: a cardinal + plural countable noun (a good twenty miles, a solid three hours) or a cardinal + measure phrase (a full two percent). The noun is plural while the article is singular, because the whole quantity is one block: ✓ a good twenty miles, and note that ✗ good twenty miles without the article is not English.
entries.with of: No of before the numeral. Of appears only in a partitive built on top: a good twenty of them.
entries.pattern: a good [cardinal] [plural noun] · a solid [cardinal] [plural noun] · an easy [cardinal] [plural noun] · a full [cardinal] [plural noun] · a good [cardinal] of [pronoun]
entries.contrast: All four mean at least, and probably more — the opposite of about, which hedges in both directions. A full is the most neutral and simply insists the count is complete (a full three days, not two and a half). A good and a solid are conversational; an easy implies the estimate is conservative (an easy two hundred people were there). Against a mere, which belittles the same number: a mere twenty miles is nothing, a good twenty miles is a haul.
entries.variants: a good many, a good few, a solid, a full, an easy, at least
entries.see also: a mere, at least, at most, about, around, roughly, approximately, no fewer than, no less than, as many as, upwards of, in excess of

entries.meaning: Marks a number as smaller or slighter than the reader might expect.
examples: The whole repair took a mere twenty minutes.
A mere two percent of applicants were accepted.
She won by a mere forty votes.
It's a mere formality at this point.
He was a mere child when the family left.
They rebuilt it in a mere three months.
entries.русский: всего лишь, каких-то — принижает количество
entries.position: a is the central determiner; mere premodifies the cardinal or the noun
entries.register: neutral to formal; rhetorical
entries.goes with: a cardinal + plural countable noun (a mere three days), a quantity phrase (a mere two percent, a mere fraction), and a singular countable noun in the non-numerical sense (a mere child, a mere formality).
entries.with of: No of before the numeral. Of appears in a partitive built on top: a mere two of the forty applicants.
entries.pattern: a mere [cardinal] [plural noun] · a mere [singular noun] · a mere [percentage/fraction] · the merest [noun]
entries.contrast: A mere does the opposite work of a good: both attach to the same number, but a mere twenty miles dismisses it and a good twenty miles respects it. As with those, the article is singular before a plural noun. Only and just hedge the same way in ordinary speech; a mere is the written, rhetorical version.
entries.variants: merely, the merest, only, just, no more than
entries.see also: a good, a solid, an easy, a full, a fraction of, about, around, roughly, approximately

entries.meaning: Introduces a number as the sum of everything counted, without hedging it in either direction.
examples: A total of forty-one applicants sat for the exam.
The county reported a total of $4.2 million in storm damage.
A total of six agencies signed the memorandum.
She missed a total of nine days all year.
A combined total of eleven inches fell across the three counties.
A total of one person objected, which is a sentence that should have read "one person objected."
entries.pronunciation note: a /ə/ and of /əv/ are weak, and the t between vowels is a flap — a total of forty is /ə ˈtoʊɾəl əv ˈfɔrti/
entries.русский: в общей сложности, всего — суммарный итог
entries.position: heads a quantity phrase in front of the numeral; the phrase then fills the determiner slot of the noun
entries.register: neutral to formal — the register of news reports, minutes, and press releases, where it is often padding
entries.type: numeral frame (summative) — it states a sum instead of hedging it
entries.goes with: a cardinal plus a plural countable noun (a total of forty-one applicants), an amount of money, time, or measure (a total of $4.2 million, a total of six hours), and a percentage. It requires a number after it: ✗ a total of applicants, ✗ a total of some people.
entries.with of: Required and fixed — part of the phrase, not a partitive: ✗ a total forty people. A real partitive is built on top with a second of: a total of nine of the twelve jurors.
entries.pattern: a total of [cardinal] [plural noun] · a total of [amount of money/time] · a total of [number] percent · a combined total of [number] · in total
entries.contrast: It hedges nothing, which is what separates it from everything else in this section: a total of forty is exactly forty, where about forty, at least forty, and up to forty are not. What it adds is that the number is a sum counted up from parts, which earns its keep in a report covering six precincts and is pure filler in A total of one person complained. Agreement follows the plural noun after of, not total: A total of forty-one applicants were interviewed, while the abstract sum takes a singular — The total was forty-one. Style guides tell writers not to begin a sentence with a numeral, and a total of exists largely to solve that problem.
entries.variants: a combined total of, in total, all told, altogether, an aggregate of, a sum of
entries.see also: at least, at most, the aggregate of, about, around, roughly, approximately, hundred, thousand, million, billion, percent

entries.meaning: Marks a number as an estimate that could fall on either side of the figure given.
examples: About twenty people showed up in the rain.
The repair will run around four hundred dollars.
Roughly half the class had already dropped.
The tank holds approximately two hundred gallons.
She got here around three o'clock, maybe a little after.
Roughly a third of the responses arrived after the deadline.
entries.русский: около, примерно, приблизительно — approximately офиц. и тех.
entries.position: premodifier of the numeral or quantity phrase — it sits outside the determiner system and takes whatever follows
entries.register: about and around neutral to conversational; roughly neutral; approximately formal and technical
entries.goes with: a cardinal + plural countable noun (about twenty people), a quantity or measure phrase (roughly two gallons, around ten percent), a fraction (about half the class), and a time expression (around three o'clock). It never attaches directly to a bare noun: ✗ about people.
entries.with of: No of of its own; it inherits whatever the quantity phrase after it requires: about a third of the class.
entries.pattern: about [cardinal] [plural noun] · around [cardinal] [plural noun] · roughly [fraction] of [noun phrase] · approximately [number] [measure noun] · about [time]
entries.contrast: These four hedge in both directions — the real number could be higher or lower — which is what separates them from a good and upwards of (at least this many) and from no more than (at most this many). Register is the only meaningful difference among the four: around is the most American and most conversational, about is the neutral default, roughly signals a deliberate rounding, and approximately belongs in specifications and lab reports. Do not stack them with the postposed hedges: ✗ about twenty or so is redundant, though it is common in speech.
entries.variants: round about (informal), some (before a round number), give or take, more or less, ballpark (informal)
entries.see also: nearly, almost, some (approximative), twenty-odd, twenty-ish, or so, a good, a solid, an easy, a full

entries.meaning: States an estimate as an open range between two numbers, with no claim about where inside it the truth sits.
examples: The job takes anywhere from two to six hours, depending on the wiring.
They're quoting anywhere from $400 to $900 for the same part.
Anywhere from twenty to thirty people usually show up on a Tuesday.
Damage estimates run anywhere from nine to fourteen million dollars.
Anywhere between a third and half the crop was lost.
Turnaround is anywhere from three days to three weeks, and they will not narrow it down.
entries.pronunciation note: both joining words are weak — from /frəm/ and to /tə/ — and the beats fall on any- and on the two numbers: anywhere from twenty to thirty /ˈɛniwɛr frəm ˈtwɛnti tə ˈθɚti/
entries.русский: где-то от … до — разг. оценка диапазона
entries.position: premodifier of a pair of numerals; it sits outside the determiner system and takes whatever quantity phrase follows
entries.register: neutral to informal — conversational and journalistic, the standard shape of an estimate from a contractor or an analyst
entries.goes with: two cardinals with a plural countable noun after the second (anywhere from twenty to thirty people), two amounts of money, time, or measure (anywhere from two to six hours), two percentages, and two fractions. The noun is stated once, after the second number. It never attaches to a bare noun: ✗ anywhere from people.
entries.with of: No of of its own; it inherits whatever the quantity phrase after it requires — anywhere from a third to half of the class.
entries.pattern: anywhere from [number] to [number] [plural noun] · anywhere from [amount] to [amount] · anywhere between [number] and [number] · anywhere from [fraction] to [fraction] of [noun phrase] · anywhere up to [number]
entries.contrast: The range is what makes the estimate honest and anywhere is what makes it wide: plain from twenty to thirty people states a range, anywhere from twenty to thirty people admits the speaker has no idea where inside it the answer falls. Keep the frame intact — anywhere between takes and, never to (✗ anywhere between twenty to thirty), and a word frame does not mix with a dash (✗ anywhere from 20–30 people → anywhere from 20 to 30 people or 20–30 people). Against up to, which names only a ceiling, and at least, which names only a floor, this one names both ends and commits to neither.
entries.variants: anywhere between … and, anywhere up to, from … to, between … and, somewhere in the range of, give or take
entries.see also: about, around, roughly, approximately, up to, at least, at most, more than, over, under, less than, twenty-odd, twenty-ish, or so

entries.meaning: Fixes the lower or upper limit of a quantity, with the stated number itself included inside the limit.
examples: There were at least forty people in line ahead of us.
The repair takes at most two days if the part is in stock.
You need at least one witness to sign the form in person.
At least half the budget was already committed by March.
She spends at most an hour a week on the newsletter.
At least three of the jurors had made up their minds before lunch.
entries.pronunciation note: at reduces to /ət/ and is never stressed here; the stress falls on least and most
entries.русский: по меньшей мере — самое большее; границы включаются
entries.position: premodifier of the numeral or quantity phrase; it sits outside the determiner system and takes whatever follows
entries.register: neutral; at least is the plainest way to state a minimum in American English
entries.goes with: a cardinal + plural countable noun (at least twenty people), a cardinal + singular countable noun when the number is one (at least one witness), a measure or money phrase (at most two gallons, at least fifty dollars), a fraction (at least half the budget), and — unusually for this section — a following determiner or quantifier (at least some warning, at most a few minutes). It never attaches to a bare noun with no quantity in it: ✗ at least people.
entries.with of: No of of its own; it inherits whatever the quantity phrase after it requires — at least three of the jurors, at most half of them.
entries.pattern: at least [cardinal] [plural noun] · at most [cardinal] [plural noun] · at least one [singular noun] · at least/at most [fraction] of [noun phrase] · at least [amount of money/time]
entries.contrast: These are the inclusive bounds, and that is what separates them from more than and under. At least twenty includes twenty; more than twenty excludes it. At most twenty includes twenty; under twenty excludes it. Against about and around, which hedge in both directions, each of these hedges in exactly one. Against no fewer than and as many as, which mark the number as surprisingly high, at least is rhetorically flat — which is why contracts, recipes, and specifications use it. Note that at least has a second life as a discourse softener with no number in sight (It's ugly, but at least it's cheap); there it is an adverb, not a numeral modifier.
entries.variants: not less than (contracts), a minimum of, a maximum of, no more than, up to, at the very least
entries.see also: more than, over, under, less than, up to, no fewer than, no less than, as many as, a good, a solid, an easy, a full, upwards of, in excess of

entries.meaning: Marks a date as approximate — the thing belongs near this year rather than exactly in it.
examples: The catalog lists it as a Shaker side chair, circa 1840.
The photograph is dated c. 1912 in the finding aid.
Her research covers Neapolitan glassmaking circa 1600 to 1650.
The deed puts the barn on the property ca. 1878.
He still dresses like a graduate student, circa 1994.
In running prose write around 1890 rather than circa 1890 unless it is a caption.
entries.pronunciation note: the second syllable is a weak schwa and never takes stress; the abbreviations c. and ca. are read aloud either as circa or simply as "about"
entries.русский: около, приблизительно (о дате) — книжн., из латыни; сокр. c. или ca.
entries.position: premodifier of a year or a date, and postposed after a noun phrase in the informal use; outside the determiner system either way
entries.register: formal and technical — museum labels, auction and dealer catalogs, academic history, genealogy, and library cataloging, abbreviated c. or ca. In running prose around 1890 says the same thing and is not mistaken for a typo.
entries.type: approximator (date hedge) — a Latin preposition, not a determiner
entries.goes with: a year or a date above all (circa 1890, c. 1650), and by extension a named period (circa the Depression). Loosely, in business speech, a round money figure (circa $2 million) — a use British commerce made ordinary and American editors still flag. It does not attach to a plain count of things: ✗ circa twenty people → about twenty people.
entries.with of: Does not take of.
entries.pattern: circa [year] · c. [year] · ca. [year] · circa [the + period noun] · [noun phrase], circa [year] (postposed)
entries.contrast: It hedges dates, and in careful use only dates. About, around, and roughly hedge anything at all (see about, around, roughly, approximately); circa narrows to the year on the object's label. The abbreviations split by field — art history and cataloging prefer ca., general publishing prefers c. — and both sit tight against the date with no comma: c. 1890, ✗ c., 1890. There is a second, arch use in American speech where circa means "back in the era of" and is hung on the end of anything: his politics, circa 1968. That one is postposed, informal, and always a little of a joke.
entries.variants: c., ca., around, about, approximately, fl. (floruit, of a person's active years), postposed circa (informal)
entries.see also: about, around, roughly, approximately, some (approximative), nearly, almost, twenty-odd, twenty-ish, or so

entries.term: more than, over, under, less than
entries.respell: MOR thuhn, OH-vur, UN-dur, LESS thuhn
entries.meaning: Places a quantity strictly above or strictly below the figure named.
examples: More than two hundred people signed the petition in a week.
Over half the seats were empty by the third inning.
The whole procedure took under an hour.
Fewer than ten of the original tenants are still in the building.
The house sold for less than half what they paid for it.
Everything on that rack is under thirty dollars.
entries.pronunciation note: than is always weak, /ðən/ or /ðn̩/, never /θæn/
entries.русский: более, свыше — менее, меньше чем; строго, без включения самого числа
entries.position: premodifier of the numeral or quantity phrase; outside the determiner system
entries.register: neutral; over and under are the conversational pair, more than and less than the written pair
entries.goes with: a cardinal + plural countable noun (more than twenty people, over a hundred entries), a measure, money, time, or distance phrase (under two gallons, over an hour, less than thirty dollars), a fraction (more than half the seats), and a percentage (under ten percent). With a plural count of separate things, careful writing prefers fewer than to less than: fewer than twenty applicants. It never attaches to a bare noun: ✗ more than people.
entries.with of: No of of its own; it inherits the requirement of whatever follows — more than half of the residents, fewer than ten of them.
entries.pattern: more than [cardinal] [plural noun] · over [cardinal] [plural noun] · fewer than [cardinal] [plural countable noun] · less than [amount/uncountable noun] · under [amount] · more than [fraction] of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The fewer/less split runs through all four. Fewer counts, less measures: fewer than twenty applicants but less than twenty dollars. Money, time, distance, and weight take less even when the number is plural, because they are single amounts rather than counts of separate things: less than five miles, less than two hours, less than ten pounds. The old objection to over meaning more than ("over is only spatial") was never a real rule and the AP Stylebook dropped it in 2014 — over a hundred entries is ordinary American English. All four bounds are exclusive: more than twenty does not include twenty. For a bound that does include it, use at least and at most.
entries.variants: fewer than, no more than, up to, north of / south of (informal, financial), better than (informal, = more than), shy of (informal, = just under)
entries.see also: at least, at most, up to, upwards of, in excess of, no fewer than, no less than, as many as, fewer, less

entries.meaning: Marks a quantity as falling just short of the figure named.
examples: Nearly a hundred commuters were stranded overnight.
Almost half the budget went to a single contractor.
Almost every seat was taken by seven o'clock.
We got nearly all of it done before the power went out.
Almost no one filled out the second page.
That's not nearly enough for a deposit.
entries.русский: почти, без малого — приближение снизу
entries.position: premodifier of a numeral, quantifier, or determiner
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: a cardinal + plural countable noun (nearly a hundred people), a fraction (almost half the budget), and — unusually for this section — a following determiner: almost every seat, nearly all the money, almost no one. It does not attach to a bare noun: ✗ nearly people.
entries.with of: No of of its own; it inherits the requirement of whatever follows: nearly all of them, almost half of the class.
entries.pattern: nearly [cardinal] [plural noun] · almost [fraction] [noun phrase] · almost every [singular noun] · nearly all [the + noun] · almost no [noun]
entries.contrast: Nearly and almost set a ceiling the number falls just short of, so they are one-directional where about and around go both ways: nearly a hundred is 95, never 105. The two are interchangeable before numbers; only almost is fully comfortable in almost every, almost no, and almost anyone, and only nearly takes not nearly (not nearly enough). Both attach to all, every, and no, but neither attaches to some: ✗ almost some.
entries.variants: not nearly, just about, close to, practically, virtually, all but
entries.see also: about, around, roughly, approximately, upwards of, in excess of, all, half

entries.term: no fewer than, no less than, as many as
entries.ipa: /noʊ ˈfjuɚ ðən/, /noʊ ˈlɛs ðən/, /əz ˈmɛni əz/
entries.respell: noh FYOO-ur thuhn, noh LESS thuhn, az MEN-ee az
entries.meaning: Marks a number as a minimum, and marks it as surprisingly large.
examples: No fewer than forty families were displaced by the fire.
The storm dropped as much as eight inches in some counties.
As many as three hundred homes may be without power tonight.
The renovation will cost no less than half a million dollars.
No fewer than six agencies have jurisdiction over that stretch of river.
The objection came from no less than the chief of staff.
entries.русский: не менее чем, целых — подчёркнутый минимум, книжн. и журн.
entries.position: premodifier of the numeral
entries.register: neutral to formal; journalistic
entries.goes with: no fewer than and as many as take a cardinal + plural countable noun (no fewer than forty applicants, as many as three hundred homes). No less than and as much as take amounts and uncountable nouns (no less than half the budget, as much as two gallons). No less than is also used before a plural count in speech (no less than forty applicants), and careful writers change it to no fewer than.
entries.with of: No of before the numeral; of comes from the partitive built on top: no fewer than half of the residents.
entries.pattern: no fewer than [cardinal] [plural noun] · no less than [amount/uncountable noun] · as many as [cardinal] [plural noun] · as much as [amount] · no less a [noun] than [name]
entries.contrast: The fewer/less split is the whole trap. Fewer counts, less measures: no fewer than twelve jurors, no less than a gallon. All three phrases mark the number as surprisingly high — they are rhetorical, not neutral, so a specification that just needs a minimum should say at least. Note the separate idiom no less than meaning "none other than": The complaint came from no less than the mayor herself.
entries.variants: at least, not less than (contracts), as few as, as little as, no more than (the ceiling version)
entries.see also: at least, at most, upwards of, in excess of, a good, a solid, an easy, a full, fewer, less

entries.meaning: Places an amount above (north of) or below (south of) a figure, in informal money talk.
examples: The renovation came in north of two million dollars.
Their approval rating is south of forty percent and still falling.
He's making north of six figures at the new firm.
The truck was doing north of ninety when it left the road.
Anything south of thirty grand isn't going to buy that lot.
She's just north of fifty and running marathons.
entries.pronunciation note: of is weak, /əv/, and reduces to /ə/ before a consonant — north of ten grand /ˈnɔrθ ə ˈtɛn ˈɡrænd/; the beat is on the compass word and on the number
entries.русский: больше чем — меньше чем; разг. и образно, обычно о деньгах
entries.position: premodifier of the numeral or amount; outside the determiner system
entries.register: informal and figurative — business talk, financial journalism, and sports commentary, where it is stock phrasing for money. It is never the register for a contract or a spec sheet.
entries.goes with: an amount of money above all (north of two million dollars), and by extension any figure people picture on a dial or a chart — an age, a speed, a percentage, a temperature (south of forty percent, north of ninety miles an hour). It also attaches to a bare figure standing alone: The bid came in north of forty. Not a bare noun: ✗ north of applicants.
entries.with of: The of is required and fixed — part of the phrase, not a partitive. To build a real partitive on top, repeat it: north of half of the fleet.
entries.pattern: north of [amount of money] · south of [amount] · north of [number] percent · just north/south of [amount] · north of [number] (standing alone)
entries.contrast: North of means more than and south of means less than, from the compass on a wall map where up is more. They belong with more than, over, under, less than and are exclusive in the same way — north of forty does not include forty — but they carry a swagger those plain words do not, which is why an annual report says in excess of and a broker says north of. They live on money. North of two hundred thousand dollars is idiomatic; north of two hundred thousand applicants is not, and counts of people and things want more than. South of is much rarer and usually turns up for the sake of the pair. The older informal better than (better than forty of them showed) does the same job.
entries.variants: just north of, just south of, better than (informal), upwards of, in excess of, shy of (= just under)
entries.see also: more than, over, under, less than, upwards of, in excess of, at least, at most, up to, -plus

entries.meaning: Marks a number as right only to the nearest round magnitude.
examples: The repair will cost on the order of ten million dollars.
They handle on the order of two hundred cases a year.
Response time is on the order of a few milliseconds.
We're talking on the order of six months, not six weeks.
The county expects on the order of five thousand new residents by 2035.
Losses ran on the order of fifteen percent across the whole portfolio.
entries.pronunciation note: the article switches form: the is /ði/ before the vowel of order, never ✗ /ðə/. On and of are weak too, /ən/ and /əv/, so everything in front of the number flattens to /ənðiˈɔrdɚəv/.
entries.русский: порядка — тех./науч.: примерно такой величины
entries.position: premodifier of the numeral or quantity phrase; outside the determiner system
entries.register: formal and technical — engineering, science writing, and analysis. In conversation the word is about.
entries.goes with: a round cardinal plus a plural countable noun (on the order of two hundred cases), an amount of money, time, or measure (on the order of ten million dollars, on the order of six months), and a percentage. Like some (approximative) it wants a round number: ✗ on the order of two hundred seven cases. Not a bare noun: ✗ on the order of cases.
entries.with of: The of is required and fixed — part of the phrase. A real partitive needs a second of: on the order of half of the fleet.
entries.pattern: on the order of [round cardinal] [plural noun] · on the order of [amount] · on the order of [number] percent · of the order of [number] (older and British)
entries.contrast: It hedges in both directions like about, but it hedges harder: about two hundred claims to be close to two hundred, while on the order of two hundred claims only the right ballpark — the right power of ten and roughly the right leading digit. That is why it sits next to an order of magnitude, which counts those powers of ten exactly. Do not confuse it with the ordinary in the order of, meaning "in sequence" (deal with them in the order of arrival); on is the American form of the hedge and of the order of is the older, more British one. And do not stack it: ✗ on the order of magnitude of ten million.
entries.variants: of the order of (British), in the ballpark of, something like, roughly, approximately, give or take
entries.see also: an order of magnitude, about, around, roughly, approximately, some (approximative), anywhere from … to, a factor of

entries.meaning: Marks a number as a floor that the real figure meets or passes, hung on the end of the number itself.
examples: She has twenty-plus years on the same beat.
The posting asks for five-plus years of supervisory experience.
Turnout was 200-plus, which nobody expected in a primary.
They handed us a 300-plus-page report the night before the vote.
Tickets ran $80-plus once the fees were added.
The 65-plus crowd votes in every municipal election.
✗ about twenty-plus people → ✓ twenty-plus people, or about twenty people.
entries.pronunciation note: it hangs on the number with no pause and takes no stress of its own, though it keeps its full vowel — twenty-plus years is /ˈtwɛnti plʌs ˈjɪrz/, with the beats on twen- and years
entries.русский: с лишним, и более — присоединяется после числа: 20-plus years — двадцать с лишним лет
entries.position: attaches after the numeral, inside the quantity phrase; the phrase then modifies the noun
entries.register: informal to neutral — journalism, job postings, résumés, and advertising, where it is compact and completely standard
entries.goes with: a cardinal plus a plural countable noun (twenty-plus applicants, 50-plus years), an amount of money, an age, or a measure ($500-plus, a 300-plus-page report), and an age band standing alone (the 65-plus crowd). It never attaches to a bare noun (✗ plus applicants), and with the number one it is unidiomatic — use one or more.
entries.with of: No of. A partitive is built separately: twenty-plus of the original crew.
entries.pattern: [cardinal]-plus [plural noun] · [cardinal]-plus (standing alone) · a [cardinal]-plus-[singular measure noun] [noun] · [amount]-plus · the [age]-plus [noun]
entries.contrast: It marks a floor, exactly like upwards of, and that is what separates it from -odd, which hedges both ways: twenty-odd years could be nineteen, twenty-plus years could not. Both are postposed, which separates them in turn from about, some, and at least, and none of them should be stacked — ✗ about twenty-plus years. Keep the hyphen: twenty-plus years is a quantity, twenty plus years reads as arithmetic. In the attributive the whole thing hyphenates and the measure noun goes singular, exactly as it does after a plain cardinal: a 30-plus-year veteran.
entries.variants: -odd, or more, and up, and counting, and change (of money and time), upwards of
entries.see also: twenty-odd, twenty-ish, or so, upwards of, in excess of, at least, at most, more than, over, under, less than, north of, south of

entries.meaning: Hedges a round number in the same way about does, in a more formal register.
examples: Some twenty people were waiting outside the courthouse.
The building has stood there some two hundred years.
Some fifty thousand ballots remain uncounted.
She left the company some three years ago.
The fire burned some forty acres before it was contained.
Some six hundred pages of testimony were entered into the record.
entries.русский: около, примерно — книжн. перед круглым числом: some fifty people
entries.position: premodifier of a round cardinal
entries.register: formal, literary, journalistic; it sounds bookish in conversation
entries.goes with: a round cardinal + plural countable noun — some twenty people, some fifty years. It does not go with a bare noun in this sense, and it does not go with a small or precise number: ✗ some three people, ✗ some twenty-two people — the number has to be a round approximation.
entries.with of: Not in this sense. The partitive some of the students is the ordinary quantifier some, a different word with a different pronunciation.
entries.pattern: some [round cardinal] [plural noun] · some [round cardinal] [plural time noun] ago · some [round cardinal] [measure noun]
entries.contrast: Pronunciation separates the two somes. The ordinary quantifier is unstressed and reduced — some water /səm ˈwɔtɚ/ — while the approximator is stressed and full: some twenty people /ˈsʌm ˈtwɛnti ˈpipəl/. Meaning separates them too: this one means about, and it is the only some that can be replaced by approximately. For the everyday quantifier, see some — this entry covers only the numeral-hedging use.
entries.variants: some … odd, about, approximately, upwards of
entries.see also: about, around, roughly, approximately, upwards of, in excess of, some, twenty-odd, twenty-ish, or so

entries.meaning: Hedges a number from behind, marking it as approximate or as a floor.
examples: There were twenty-odd people in the waiting room.
Give me ten minutes or so and I'll be ready.
He's fortyish, maybe a little younger.
She's been teaching there thirty-odd years.
We're meeting at sixish if that works.
It cost two hundred dollars or so, plus tax.
entries.русский: двадцать с чем-то, где-то двадцать, примерно — разг., ставится после числа
entries.position: attaches after the numeral, not before it
entries.register: informal; -odd is neutral in speech and casual writing, -ish is conversational
entries.goes with: a cardinal + plural countable noun (twenty-odd people), or a bare numeral or time expression standing alone (twenty or so, around fiveish). -ish also attaches to times and ages (sixish, fortyish).
entries.with of: No of. The partitive is built separately: twenty-odd of them.
entries.pattern: [cardinal]-odd [plural noun] · [cardinal] or so · [cardinal] or so [plural noun] · [cardinal]-ish · [cardinal] odd years · [cardinal] or thereabouts
entries.contrast: The hyphen in -odd carries meaning. Twenty-odd people means about twenty; twenty odd people means twenty peculiar people. Always hyphenate. -odd attaches only to round numbers and always means "a bit more" — twenty-odd is never nineteen. Or so and -ish hedge in both directions like about, and -ish alone can answer a question ("What time?" "Sixish."). All three are postposed, which is what distinguishes them from about and some, and they should not be stacked with those: ✗ about twenty-odd people.
entries.variants: or thereabouts, give or take, -something (twenty-something), and change (twenty dollars and change), plus (twenty plus)
entries.see also: about, around, roughly, approximately, some (approximative), up to, upwards of, in excess of

entries.meaning: Sets an inclusive ceiling: anything from nothing at all up to the figure named.
examples: The van holds up to twelve passengers.
Shipping takes up to six business days.
They're advertising up to fifty percent off, which guarantees almost nothing.
Are you allowed up to two carry-ons on this fare?
The grant covers up to half the tuition.
The fine can run up to five thousand dollars.
Each household may register up to one vehicle per space.
It doesn't hold up to two gallons, whatever the box says.
entries.pronunciation note: to is weak, /tə/, and never carries stress; the beats fall on up and on the number — up to twenty /ˌʌp tə ˈtwɛnti/
entries.русский: до, вплоть до — верхняя граница включительно
entries.position: premodifier of the numeral or quantity phrase; it sits outside the determiner system and takes whatever follows
entries.register: neutral; the standard way to state a ceiling in advertising, specifications, and warranties
entries.goes with: a cardinal + plural countable noun (up to twenty passengers), a measure, money, or time phrase (up to two gallons, up to fifty dollars, up to six hours), a fraction (up to half the class), and a percentage (up to forty percent). With the number one it takes a singular countable noun, as any one-phrase does: up to one guest per resident. It never attaches to a bare noun with no quantity in it: ✗ up to passengers, ✗ up to money.
entries.with of: No of of its own; it inherits whatever the quantity phrase after it requires — up to half of the residents, up to three of the four seats, up to ten percent of the total.
entries.pattern: up to [cardinal] [plural noun] · up to one [singular noun] · up to [amount of money/time] · up to [fraction] of [noun phrase] · up to [number] percent · up to and including [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: It sets a ceiling, not an estimate, and that is exactly what advertising trades on. Up to fifty percent off promises nothing but the ceiling — one item marked down fifty percent satisfies it. Like at most the bound is inclusive: up to twenty includes twenty, where under twenty and fewer than twenty exclude it. Against about and around, which hedge in both directions, up to hedges only downward — the real figure can be anything from nothing at all up to the number named. That is also what separates it from upwards of, which points the other way and means more than. In contracts, the fuller up to and including removes any doubt about whether the endpoint counts.
entries.variants: up to and including, at most, no more than, a maximum of, not to exceed (contracts), as many as (the rhetorical version)
entries.see also: at least, at most, more than, over, under, less than, no fewer than, no less than, as many as, about, around, roughly, approximately, upwards of, in excess of

entries.meaning: Marks the stated number as a lower bound that the real figure passes.
examples: Upwards of two hundred people applied for six positions.
The verdict was in excess of ten million dollars.
The drive takes upwards of six hours in summer traffic.
Losses in excess of the deductible are covered.
Upwards of forty percent of the fleet is out of service.
They've raised upwards of a million dollars since March.
entries.русский: свыше, более — in excess of юр. и фин.
entries.position: premodifier of the numeral; of is part of the fixed phrase
entries.register: upwards of neutral to journalistic; in excess of formal, legal, and financial
entries.goes with: a cardinal + plural countable noun (upwards of two hundred applicants) and a cardinal + measure or amount phrase (in excess of ten million dollars, upwards of six hours). Not a bare noun: ✗ upwards of applicants.
entries.with of: The of is required and fixed — it is part of the phrase, not a partitive. To build a real partitive on top, repeat it: upwards of half of the residents.
entries.pattern: upwards of [cardinal] [plural noun] · in excess of [cardinal] [measure noun] · upwards of [cardinal] percent · upward of [cardinal] (variant spelling)
entries.contrast: Both mean more than the number given, which puts them with no fewer than, against the two-directional about, and directly opposite up to — up to two hundred is a ceiling, upwards of two hundred is a floor, and swapping them reverses the claim. Upwards of has a second, looser use in American speech meaning "roughly, and probably a bit more" (upwards of an hour), so avoid it where the number is a legal threshold. In excess of is the contract-and-annual-report register and always means strictly greater than; in plain prose more than says the same thing in two syllables.
entries.variants: upward of, over, more than, north of (informal, financial), better than (informal)
entries.see also: no fewer than, no less than, as many as, more than, over, under, less than, up to, about, around, roughly, approximately, a good, a solid, an easy, a full, some (approximative)
